2.	What are the various elements making up the present cost-of-living index?
3.	In the prospective cost-of-living index, what changes are going to be made as far as the addition of further elements is concerned, or the removal of any now included?

speechtext:
Composition of the present cost of living index:
1. Purpose. The dominion bureau of statistics cost of living index measures the influence of changes in retail prices of goods and services, upon the cost of a representative urban wage earner family budget.
Each index figure is a percentage which shows the relationship between the dollar cost of the index budget at a specified time, and the corresponding cost of the same budget in a reference period. The bureau's reference period now is the five-year interval 1935 to 1939, and the average cost of the index budget for this period is represented by 100-0. The comparable cost at March 1, 1952 was 189-1 per cent of its base period cost. This figure of 189-1 becomes the cost of living index for March, 1952.
The index budget. The index budget was calculated from annual purchases reported by a group of 1,439 typical wage earner families in the following cities: Charlottetown, Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal,

Questions
Ottawa, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Vancouver. These expenditures covered the year ending September, 1938.
The survey families averaged 4-6 persons and the majority had two or three children. Family earnings in many cases were supplemented by minor sources of income; total
incomes for these families were heavily concentrated between $1,200 and $1,600. They ranged, however, from as low as $600 up to about $2,800 per annum. There were approximately two tenant families to every one home-owning family, and about one family in three operated a motorcar.

Group index numbers
The index budget is divided into six expenditure groups for which separate indexes are calculated; these are foods, fuel and light, rent, clothing, home furnishings and services, and miscellaneous items. Each group contains a list of items sufficiently large to make it representative of the merchandise field covered. It would be possible to add many more minor items without affecting the movements of the composite cost of living index by any significant amount. These additions would lengthen the time required to calculate the index and impose a greater burden upon firms making price reports, without improving the accuracy of the index. In many cases accuracy might be reduced, as comparisons on a quality basis are not possible over a long period. This would be true of style merchandise such as women's hats. The cost of all these omitted items is included in group weights, which represent all expenditures falling within the six groups noted above. The base period food weight of 31 per cent, for example, was calculated from total food costs reported by survey families, although the food index 
includes only 46 items which represent about 75 per cent of a representative family's food expenditure.
Foods. Prices used in calculating food indexes are collected on the first business day of each month from approximately 1,600 stores covering independent and chain grocers and butchers. Quotations for each of the 46 budget items are averaged and then multiplied by the budget quantity for each individual item to find the cost for that item. These individual cost figures are added together to find the total cost of the food budget; this figure is then expressed as a percentage of the corresponding reference period cost to produce the food index.
Fuel and light. Separate indexes are calculated for coal, coke, gas and electricity. The two last mentioned are reckoned from monthly bills for quantities which are typical of consumption in the cities represented. The bill for each city is weighted by the number of domestic consumers in order to calculate dominion indexes. The coal index also takes account of typical amounts consumed in different areas and of the population of each city represented in the index. Price changes

for coal are related to kinds used in the greatest quantity in each area.
Shelter. Changes in shelter costs are determined by movements of rents. Since 1948 changes in shelter costs have been determined by data obtained from rent surveys inaugurated by the special surveys division of the dominion bureau of statistics. The surveys are taken four times a year, in March, June, August and November. The rent index is calculated from a matched sample of households. That is, the aggregate rent paid by a group of households at a given point in time is compared with the aggregate rent paid by the same group of households for the same living quarters at the next point in time. By using a matched sample for each survey period, variations due to changes in the sample and to non-response are eliminated. The index is, therefore, a measure of the change of rent paid for the same accommodation. Rent reported is the cash rent paid in all cases regardless of minor changes in the services provided. Serious difficulties are involved in attempting to assess the money value of services, such as those provided by janitors, and it is not practical to attempt to adjust the index for variations in the amenities or services provided by the landlord. However, when there are changes in the amount of accommodation or space rented, the cases are eliminated from the comparison. Rent for commercial premises is specifically excluded from the calculation of the index. Thus, cases in which the rent covers both living quarters and commercial space are excluded from the aggregates from which the index is calculated. Usually, the rent index is not adjusted until one month after each survey period.
Clothing. The clothing index has been based upon a carefully selected list of men's and women's apparel. It includes no children's clothing, and omits some items of adult clothing which are of considerable importance, such as women's dresses for afternoon and evening wear, women's hats, men's hats and gloves. Unusual difficulties in maintaining continuous price series on the same quality of goods occur in clothing due to style and seasonal changes which must be excluded from price comparisons based upon quality. The items in the clothing index have been selected to represent the basic materials entering into clothing in approximately the same proportions as they would be found in a complete clothing budget. Some of the items chosen to represent basic materials form a comparatively small portion of a complete budget, but are useful in measuring clothing
Questions
price trends because of their standard construction. Women's woollen hose afford an example of such items. The index contains 33 items of clothing, piece goods and footwear, and price series for these have been examined individually over a period of years to test their reliability. Most apparel now is composed of six basic materials, cotton, wool, rayon, nylon, leather and rubber. The bureau uses a clothing list of 33 items with the knowledge that a limited but accurate price series will measure the trend of clothing prices better than a large list including items which fluctuate widely in price due to style and seasonal factors. Department stores are the source of bureau clothing prices. These distributors handle approximately one-third of the dominion's clothing trade, and make monthly price returns to the bureau, especially designed for the cost of living index.
The bureau of statistics Is concerned not only with the accuracy of prices reported, but also with the comparative quality of goods priced from month to month. It considers a decline in quality to have the same effect upon living costs as a rise in price. Field representatives have been given special instructions and training regarding this matter, and price schedules for clothing and home furnishings have been specially designed for the reporting of quality changes in addition to the recording of comparative prices.
Home furnishings and services. The home furnishings and services index is a composite of nine subgroups, including two sets of service costs in addition to actual furnishings. The nine subgroups are: furniture, electrical equipment, floor coverings, textiles furnishings, hardware, dishes and glassware, cleaning supplies, laundry and telephone. The complete group accounted for 9 per cent of the base period index budget cost, placing it next to clothing in importance. It is similar to clothing also in many details of construction. The data for furniture, electrical equipment, floor coverings, textile furnishings, hardware, dishes and glassware are obtained from department stores and the same principle of the representation of basic materials by a comparatively small number of items is used. There are 8 items of furniture, 3 of electrical equipment, 3 of floor coverings, 4 of textile furnishings, 6 of hardware, 2 of dishes and glassware, 4 of cleaning supplies, 3 laundry rates, and one type of telephone service.
Miscellaneous. Five subgroups, health maintenance, personal care, transportation, recreation and life insurance comprise the miscellaneous index. This list does not exhaust all remaining family living expend-

itures, but most of those which are left, such as church contributions, support of dependents, etc., cannot be treated in the same way as items which are bought and sold. The index takes no account of these items which amounted to only 3 per cent of average wage-earner family living expenditures reported in the bureau's 1938 survey.
The health section is based upon prices for 6 items of household medical supplies, 2 kinds of hospital service, 3 types of doctors' fees, and rates for 6 types of dental service. In view of the stability of fees for doctors, dentists and hospitals, these records are collected only at annual intervals, while medical supplies are priced quarterly. Records of practically all miscellaneous subindexes are collected from 23 of the larger cities, chosen to give adequate regional representation.
Personal care costs are represented by 9 items of toilet requirements plus fees for men's haircuts and shaves.
Three kinds of transportations are represented in the transportation subgroup: motor car, street car and railway. The two latter present no special problems, but motor car operating costs are more difficult to measure. The bureau's record is based upon service station prices of gasoline, licence fees, tires and wage rates for garage mechanics. It is assumed that depreciation is 35 per cent of operating costs, and that for car owners as a group it remains constant from year to year.
The recreation section includes records of motion pictures theatre admissions, and newspaper, magazine and tobacco costs.
The life insurance index is based upon premiums for ordinary non-participating life policies, since these appear to give the closest possible approximation to the cost of pure risk. Averages of premiums for ages 20, 35 and 50 years have been used covering the records of 11 large companies.
The Cost of Living Index Calculation
There are two stages in the calculation of each of the six principal group indexes from which the composite number is calculated. In the first stage, the general procedure is to multiply current price averages by budget quantities. These products are added together and the resultant aggregate divided by a corresponding base period aggregate. This number is multiplied by 100-0 to secure a subgroup index for the current period. The index is then multiplied by a subgroup weight indicative of the cost of goods in this subgroup relative to all goods in the group. When all subgroups have been weighted similarly, the group index is found by adding up this second set of products and dividing by 100-0. This routine is repeated to secure the final composite cost of living index. The second and third stages of weighting are made necessary by the fact that it is not feasible to include all items in the family budget.

Final decisions remain to be made on a few items in the new budget, but in total the new index will be calculated from prices of approximately 225 items as compared with the present list of 160. Additions to foods will include a considerable number of fresh fruits and vegetables; and items of children's wear will be added to the clothing index. In addition to rents it is planned to price the principal home-ownership costs if certain technical difficulties can be overcome. Fuel oil will be added and the list of household equipment and services has been expanded. The Other Commodities and Services index will include a number of additional items, in particular, a wider representation for transportation and recreation. Life insurance premiums will be dropped because they include a large element Of savings, while the other major element, risk, is related to future rather than current purchasing power measurements. Additional information concerning the new consumer price index will be found in the attached statement.

The New Consumer Price Index
(Reprinted from the Daily Bulletin, March 14, 1952, for your information)
During the latter half of 1951 the dominion bureau of statistics held numerous meetings with groups and organizations to explain and discuss the plans for the revised index which is to be renamed more accurately the consumer price index. The groups and organizations included not only a wide variety of interests but also competent technical opinion. They represented consumers, labour, management, farmers, and professional economists. In addition, it has been possible to discuss the most up-to-date techniques for constructing consumer price indexes with experts of several countries which have highly developed statistical organizations. During the course of these discussions it was decided to use 1949 as a base period and work resulting from this decision will require several months to complete. Therefore, publication will not commence before the summer of 1952, at which time a comprehensive explanation of the index will be issued. The present statement outlines briefly some of the main features which appear to have wide public interest.

Purpose and title.
The main purpose of the revision has been to bring up to date the list of items and quantities included in the index budget and to place the series on a post-war base. Thus there will be no change in the fundamental purpose of the index which is to measure changes in the prices which the consumer pays for goods and services.
While the title, "cost-of-living index", has historically been used to describe indexes which serve this purpose, it has proved confusing, and will therefore be changed to "consumer price index". This change in title is one which is being adopted widely in other countries and is made to clarify the real purpose of the index, that is, to measure changes in prices of a representative basket of goods and services.
Base period.
The post-war period selected as the base for the new index is the calendar year 1949, and the index for that year will be 100. Since prices were higher in 1949 than they were in the period 1935-39, which is the base of the present index and which now equals 100, the new index numbers will be lower, of course, than if they were on the 1935-39 base. This does not mean that prices have risen less; the percentage change in the price level shown by the new index would be the same from month to month whichever base is used.
The index budget.
In determining the items to be included in the budget it was first necessary to decide what families should be selected from the nation-wide sample of household expenditures collected for the year ending September 1948, and supplemented by four food surveys in October 1948 and March, June and September 1949. The new index has been designed to reflect the experience of families located in 27 cities, each having more than 30,000 population. They ranged in size from two adults to two adults with four children and the annual incomes of these households during the survey year ranged from $1,650 to $4,050 with the majority of incomes between $2,000 and $3,000.
The income and size limitations were selected to secure a wide coverage within which expenditure patterns could be adequately represented by the same price index. The families have not been restricted to those with wage earner heads. Actual tests showed that expenditure patterns of households with wage earner heads were almost identical with those of other urban families within the same size and income
Questions
ranges. This is not surprising when it is considered that wage earners and non-wage earners are found living on the same streets, buying in the same stores, and generally living in the same manner. It was thus possible to include families with all types of income, without making the index less representative of wage earners.
Although there have been considerable changes between pre-war and post-war purchasing habits, the general pattern of spending has altered surprisingly little. Changes in the classification of items to give more useful group indexes prevent exact comparison of the old and new index patterns, but the degree of similarity can be judged from the following summary table. The new household operation group compares roughly with a combination of the two series for fuel and light and home furnishings and services. Likewise, the new other commodities and services group contains many of the items listed in the present index under miscellaneous.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EMBARGOES ON SHIPMENTS

I think I stated yesterday-if I did not, I will state it now-that we have a definite understanding with all the provinces that we shall be permitted to exercise even the authority which the provinces think is their responsibility with respect to the marketing of meat as long as the United States embargo remains in effect. This arrangement has been functioning fairly satisfactorily.
Occasionally we have representations made by the provinces to the effect that something that is being done is not working as smoothly as it might. There was an arrangement made between the packing houses at Edmonton, Calgary, I think Lethbridge, and Vancouver, a day or two ago with our consent and more or less under our direction. Instructions were issued1 to both railways yesterday in the same terms. One railway interpreted them

a little differently from the other. One railway kept on shipping meat and the other did not. This was reported to us, and inside of a few hours at the outside they were both operating in the same way, namely, taking beef through to Vancouver. How the article got into the newspapers without the correction I do not know, but the whole matter was settled yesterday and there were no difficulties such as were outlined in the papers this morning for any length of time whatsoever.

speechtext: The parliamentary assistant will know that it is in no personal sense that I begin by asking whether we are to deal with these resolutions without the benefit of the minister. We have raised that question before, and I raise it again now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This has been decided in the past. We have four resolutions here, one dealing with the Excise Tax Act, one with the Excise Act, one with income tax and one with succession duties. For convenience they are broken down into paragraphs. The practice has been to consider them paragraph by paragraph; but taking the excise tax resolution as an example, the vote will be on the resolution as a whole.
So far as the other point is concerned, I rather anticipated that it would be raised so 
I looked up the record to see how these budget resolutions have been piloted through the house in recent years. I find that when the present Minister of Finance was parliamentary assistant to Mr. Ilsley in 1944 and 1945, he did the job of piloting the resolutions through. After all, they are only indications in principle of the changes which will be presented to the house later in the various bills amending these acts. I have been assistant to the present minister for four budgets now, and on each of those occasions it has been the practice to have me discuss the resolutions. In his budget speech the minister spent considerable time on the principle, and of course later when the bills are before the house he will be here to deal with them in detail.
Getting back to the original point on how we will consider these resolutions we have had a vote in this house on this very matter. We have before us four resolutions, each of which is divided into various paragraphs; but the actual vote will be on each entire resolution, not on any paragraph of any one of them.
I would like to ask the parliamentary assistant if he intends to proceed with these resolutions in the absence of the leader of the opposition.

I understand that in the Department of National Revenue, particularly in the customs and excise division, there is a different method of paying employees for overtime from that followed in connection with the regular monthly or semi-monthly cheques. My information is that in some instances these employees have to wait a very long time for their overtime pay. Will the parliamentary assistant look into that matter and give the committee any information he can find, at an appropriate time? I would like him to indicate how long they have to wait for their overtime pay, and whether there is not some method by which that difficulty could be remedied so that they could get their overtime pay in the ordinary way when they get their regular cheques.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Of course this question has nothing whatever to do with the four resolutions now before the committee, nor with the Department of Finance. Then perhaps my hon. friend would be a kind of honorary messenger for me and see that this request gets to the right place.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wonder if I might say a word about the procedure we are following in connection with these budget resolutions. I recognize the correctness of the statement made by the parliamentary assistant to the effect that on at least two previous occasions, if not more, the house has decided by a vote that there must be only one vote on the entire resolution, no matter how many paragraphs it contains. No one in this committee will suggest that I agreed with that decision. I disagreed with it strongly; I still think the house made an incorrect decision, but we seem to have no alternative but to abide by it.
Nevertheless I think we must all recognize that it would lead to a most disorderly debate if we were to wander all over the eight or ten paragraphs into which, in the language of the parliamentary assistant, some of these resolutions are broken down. So I suggest that even if we are not given the right to vote on these paragraphs seriatim, they should be discussed seriatim so that it will be in some sort of order. I would urge, Mr. Chairman, that you find some language on the basis of which you could call for the discussion of these various paragraphs one at a time.
One other point has been mentioned, and I would like to say a word on it while I am on my feet. I recognize the fact that in a good many sessions it has been the practice for the parliamentary assistant to do some of the work of the Minister of Finance, particularly at this stage of the budget proceedings. After all, that is what parliamentary assistants are for, to take some of the load off the shoulders of their ministers. I suggest that with respect to some of these resolutions, at least with respect to some of the paragraphs in some of these resolutions, pretty important issues are involved. I would hope that if we reach an issue about which some of us feel pretty strongly, the discussion might be allowed to stand until we can have the minister here.
I hope you will not call me to order if I mention, merely as an example of what I now have in mind, paragraph 5 of the resolution respecting the Income Tax Act. It has to do with medical expenses. As the parliamentary assistant knows, we have already had considerable discussion about that matter in this house, and on one or two occasions he spoke for the Minister of Finance. As the house knows, we got into considerable confusion over that whole matter; and I feel
Excise Tax Act
that when we reach that subject we should have the right to discuss it not with the parliamentary assistant but with the responsible minister himself.
That is the paragraph about which I feel most strongly. There may be other items in these resolutions about which other members feel strongly; and I suggest that while it would be in order for us to proceed to discuss some of these matters with the parliamentary assistant, if hon. members really want to discuss important issues with the Minister of Finance, that is our right and privilege.

I want to add just a word on the question of method. Some of us felt very strongly last year that the decision to take the items concerning the Excise Tax Act, for example, in one resolution worked, shall I say, an unfairness from our point of view, because it meant that members had no opportunity to indicate their objection to any particular item without voting against the whole resolution. However, that was done last year. I am not going to pursue the matter further now except to say that I do not think it should be regarded in any way as being accepted as a precedent. For my part I am merely refraining from putting it to the test at the moment.
I do not propose to make any extended preliminary remarks concerning the Excise Tax Act. After all, we have here in a measure an act of repentance; and repentance, as far as it goes, is an attractive thing. Even though the minister is not here to receive our congratulations on his repentance, we will, as I say, go that length with him.
With regard to the sales tax, of course there was no repentance there. We have a gesture here under paragraph 9 concerning certain articles on which the sales tax has been repealed, and when we come to that paragraph I hope to find out just what that means and just what the amounts involved are. In the meantime, I should like to ask, under paragraph 1, what is the amount involved? What amount was collected under that, and what is it expected we shall realize under the new rate?
Is the parliamentary assistant going to answer that now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Again I am in the hands of the house as to the way in which hon. members want these answers given. I can give them in groups or individually, but if it is done individually I shall be up and down all the time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It would appear as though, for the convenience of members, it might be preferable to accept the suggestion that has

Excise Tax Act
been made by the parliamentary assistant and apparently agreed upon by the spokesmen for the other parties, that is, to consider the resolution as a whole for the purpose of a vote, but for the purposes of detailed discussion to call the paragraphs seriatim.

1 believe it will be a little difficult to stick very closely to that particular method of dealing with this resolution, because one may wish at the beginning to make some remarks that will have general application; and that is what I wish to do.
Generally I think the house welcomes this resolution, because, as the hon. member for Greenwood has said, it is in the nature of an act of repentance for some of the taxes that were imposed last year.
Since the excise and sales tax are the hidden taxes which raise such enormous amounts of money, I was interested to get in the mail today an analysis made by a representative of the Winnipeg Tribune and published in their issue of last Saturday, May 3. Apparently this newspaper sent out one of its representatives to make house-to-house calls in the city of Winnipeg, and he called upon some fifteen modest homes of persons whose incomes were not high. It is interesting to note what this investigator found regarding the tax situation. A breakdown showed that the total income of these fifteen homes, the income of the men and women-in one case the joint incomes of a married couple, but usually individuals-was $65,400. The income tax paid amounted to $5,122; city tax amounted to $3,458. Interestingly enough, the computation-leaving out such things as amusement taxes levied by the city-showed that the hidden taxes paid by those who lived in these houses amounted to $5,229. In other words, the hidden taxes on the group of people interviewed, who, as I say, were in the very moderate, or perhaps in one or two cases what I would term the low income groups, were higher than the taxes levied directly through income tax.
I am not going to put it on the record, but a complete break-down will be found in the Saturday edition of the Winnipeg Tribune at page 5. The incomes of these fifteen families range from $1,500 to $5,900, the latter being the highest income in that group. They were a very representative group, and the survey indicates clearly that the hidden taxes are greater than the direct taxes. These are the taxes of which most people thoroughly disapprove. The occupations were: carpenter, switchboard operator, shipper, salesman, stenographer, three school teachers, one music teacher, accountant, assistant bank manager, bus driver, two secretaries, auditor, retired police officer, and [The Chairman.]
agent. Those were the occupants of the fifteen small houses the photographs of which appear on the front page of this newspaper.
The comprehensive analysis and table found on page 5 of the Winnipeg Tribune clearly indicates that the taxes on clothing, cigarettes, household furniture and other appliances exceed the income taxes paid by those individuals. No wonder that many people in the country prefer the direct income tax, because these excise taxes which we are discussing this afternoon do bear very heavily indeed on the people in the moderate and lower income groups.
I know it is argued that the larger the income the more of certain things people buy. But these taxes are levied not only on luxuries but on ordinary household necessities such as boots and shoes and a wide range of furnishings. I am very happy to see that this resolution does to some extent rectify the situation, although I should add only slightly.
The sales tax is being repealed on drinks prepared from milk or eggs, and up to this time they have borne the tax; on preserved fruits, which have borne the tax up to this time. Many times in this house we heard that food was exempt from the sales tax. The tax is being repealed also on cooking oils and salad oils, but not including mayonnaise or salad dressing. It is being repealed on some farm commodities, such as baling wire for baling farm produce, and steel pens for farm animals. The fishing industry will benefit by the repeal of the tax on preservatives for use exclusively in treating nets, ropes and lines. The tax is being repealed also on clays and earth for use exclusively as filtering materials in the refining of petroleum oils, and on the goods enumerated in customs tariff items 411a, 437 and 476b.
What I am pointing out is that I am glad to see that relief, but it does rather discount the statement made in this house from time to time that foods were not taxed. Certain drinks prepared from eggs and milk are used extensively in the feeding of invalids, and preserved fruit is used in a good many homes throughout the country. Of course, salad oils and cooking oils are now used extensively in the preparation of food in households as well as in restaurants and other places. I welcome that change, but it does indicate that although we were told from time to time that the sales tax did not apply to food, here we have a group of foods upon which the sales tax has been levied, and that tax is to an extent being repealed.

What I rose to say was that these hidden taxes in particular have imposed a greater burden, relatively, on the low income and middle income groups than on the higher income groups. I do not want to traverse the ground that I traversed in the budget debate itself, but I am glad that the excise taxes are being repealed in a number of instances or reduced in a number of others. I suppose the tax on automobiles is being reduced substantially because it has been difficult to sell automobiles. I rather suspect, however, that there may be another reason, that reason being that there is a rather important by-election in the county of Ontario in which the great motor centre of Oshawa is situated. I do not know, but very often we find that something of this sort is done when an election or by-election is in sight. It is an interesting coincidence, but of course it may not be more than a coincidence. Far be it from me to suggest-although I might think it-that the government would do anything of that sort in view of forthcoming by-elections.
The reductions that are made in these taxes are welcomed by the committee. The criticism I am making is that in most instances they do not go far enough; we still have these hidden taxes imposed, and they are quite substantial taxes. That is particularly true, of course, with regard to the sales tax. Even if two per cent of it has been earmarked for a desirable purpose, it is still 10 per cent in aggregate, namely eight per cent for federal revenue and two per cent for the special purpose.
While we are supporting the resolution because it reduces the impact of such taxes, I want to say that none the less we feel that this is the wrong way in which to raise revenue for the country; it is a method which is not based on the principle that most of us I am sure really at heart believe in, namely, the principle of the ability to pay. We shall have more to say when the individual paragraphs are discussed.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say a word in general about the proposals involved in this resolution concerning the excise tax. We too welcome the relief from what had become an almost intolerable situation, that is to be found in the terms of this resolution. I should like to support what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said, namely, that the hidden taxes in many instances have become heavier as a burden than are the direct taxes. That fact has been known for quite some time.
There is another evil involved in the imposition of the indirect taxes as we have been using them to raise revenue and it is this.
Excise Tax Act
In the main they are imposed at the manufacturer's level. Because of the fact that they are imposed at that level, by the time the consumer pays the final price the tax is pyramided several times. In a number of instances it can be proved without doubt that, in addition to the tax received by the government, there is also a shadow tax which pushes the price up but which the government does not get. It goes to inflate profits.
While I am not against a reasonable profit, I certainly am opposed to any taxation scheme that will inflate those profits and cause the ultimate consumer to have to pay more than he ought to pay for the goods that he buys, particularly those things that he requires to buy from day to day and from year to year in the ordinary process of living. That is one of the great objections that we have to the excise taxes as they are used by this government.
As to the economic effects of the taxes, I think it can be shown that the government could use the ultimate purchaser's tax, receive the same revenue and yet not do the economy half the harm that they are doing to it with these indirect or hidden taxes imposed at the manufacturer's level. To get away from that pyramiding I would strongly urge that we avoid hidden taxes and adopt an ultimate purchaser's tax. I know the arguments against that procedure. I know that if the consumer pays the tax and sees that it is added to the marked price, he wants to kick the dickens out of the government. I know that argument; but it does not get away from the fact that it is preferable that the tax be collected as an ultimate purchaser's tax and be remitted to the government rather than have the bad effects that the present tax method now imposes upon the economy.
It is often argued that if the excise tax is made to apply at the consumer's level we shall have to deal with many more people and will make many more people collectors of taxes. As a matter of fact that is true. But most people throughout the country who are in business are collectors of taxes for the government anyway. They are certainly collecting income taxes. They are having to make deductions at the source, and they have to make volumes of returns to the government. It would be a simple additional matter for them to make a return on the ultimate purchaser's tax. If the employers of labour across the country who are in business are given to understand that they are asked to do this in the interests of the economy of the country rather than for the purpose of imposing upon them an additional burden, I am quite sure that they would not protest at having to do the job.

Excise Tax Act
However, as has already been said, if the government persists in following its present taxation methods it will certainly persist in pyramiding prices beyond reasonable levels. That is a thing that concerns a great many people across this country.
As I say, we welcome the relief that has been provided in the resolution. I was greatly disappointed to see that the plea 1 made a year ago, and also this year during the budget debate went unheeded. On both occasions I asked that careful consideration be given to placing on the free list such materials as the concentrated vitamin E products. I do not see them under paragraph 9. I want to point out that since I spoke last year on this subject in the course of the budget debate I have investigated much further into this whole matter and have concluded that the work being done on these concentrated vitamin E products is exceedingly valuable. It is the type of work that cannot be done by any other method, apparently. I went down to the University of Ottawa to hear Dr. Shute present an illustrated lecture on this subject. He used coloured photographs-which, by the way, cannot be camouflaged. Coloured photographs are difficult to touch over; they therefore showed the actual situation as they existed before and after. His lecture, together with other information that I have been able to get, convinced me beyond a shadow of a doubt that the di-alpha tocopherols are exceedingly valuable in treating heart and vascular diseases. There are in Canada today many people who are receiving great relief from those conditions through the use of heroic doses of di-alpha tocopherol in various forms. I am quite well aware of the fact that the Canadian Medical Association has not yet placed its seal of approval on di-alpha tocopherol and the claims of the discoverers with regard to its uses in heart and vascular cases. I realize that, but I am also fully aware of the fact that a reasonable investigation has not yet been made by the medical association. That is a fact, and it can be proven. But the results of the treatment can be proven also. They show beyond doubt that this substance is most valuable. The tragedy of the situation is that when cases become quite advanced the only way relief can come to the patient is through his taking these heroic doses day after day for the rest of his life. That means a very large outlay, because the cost of the substance is high. It has to be brought across the boundary line from Rochester, where it is distilled from wheat germ; and it has to pay a duty. Before it can be brought

into the country for sale it has to pay a sales tax on the duty paid price, which boosts the cost to these people beyond their ability to pay.
An association has been formed in this country known as the Vitamin E Society of Canada. As a matter of fact, one of the members on the Liberal side of the house is the president. He and his own family have had evidence of the value of this substance in the treatment of heart and vascular diseases. It seems to me that the pleas of a group of 1,500 people who make up that society should not be just turned aside lightly. That is not all. It can be shown that more than 1,500 medical men in the country are prescribing the substance-well, a year ago they were prescribing it; if they have continued, it means in fact that they have found it is valuable in the treatment of these heart and vascular disorders.
I am hoping that before we get through the discussion of these resolutions the minister, or his assistant, will give -assurance that careful consideration will be given to putting this substance on the free list so far as sales tax and customs duty are concerned, so that these poor people who have to buy the material to get any relief whatever, or indeed to keep themselves alive, may get away from paying the very heavy price they now pay for it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I can answer two or three questions now. The hon. member for Greenwood asked first of all the total revenue involved in the past year in this particular excise tax. The amount is a little more than $150 million. The revenue reduction during the present fiscal year, 1952-53, will be $55,900,000, and a reduction when applied over the full year-that is next year-will be $61,700,000.

Is that the
reduction?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is the reduction. The total revenue for the past year was a little over $150 million.
So far as the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar are concerned, I regret I did not read this article in the Winnipeg Tribune, but two things struck me immediately about it. I think that any statistician in the country would be very dubious about any survey made on an examination of only fifteen samples. Here our bureau of statistics like to take a very large number of cases in surveys so that a proper average can be obtained. The second point which I am a little surprised at is the ability of a newspaperman to actually get down to a figure apparently as closely as he has done to show the impact on the individual of the federal

sales tax and excise tax which are not levied, of course, at the retail level but back at the manufacturer's level, where the individual has no knowledge. This is a calculation which the statisticians in our department and in the department of the bureau of statistics have considerable difficulty in estimating.
The third point is of course perhaps a good demonstration of the difficulties and fallacies of sampling just one group-in this case low-income families. For example, take a married man with two children. For ease of calculation we will take two children not in receipt of family allowances, so there will not be any compensating factor of exemption for family allowances. This man has to earn more than $2,800 a year before he pays any income tax. So that you could say that that man is entirely taxed indirectly. He is paying one hundred per cent indirect taxes to the federal government. That would be a pretty alarming statement. On the other hand, we can say with pride that this situation develops because this man receives the highest income tax exemptions of any country in the world.
At the other extreme this reporter could have gone to the rich men in Winnipeg-I do not know which part of the city they live in-and interviewed them, and he would have found that about ninety-nine per cent of their taxes were direct taxes, because of course the direct income tax is so heavily progressive in the upper brackets that-
The impact of the higher taxes would not be as great on that man as on the man in the low-income group.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mainly because the impact of this violently progressive system of income tax is so terrific on that man. The best way to get the national average, to see the national impact of the direct taxes against indirect taxes, is by using the illustration which I am very grateful to the hon. member for Peace River for provoking me into finding out. That is the study of the change in incidence of tax since this government took power. I mentioned that in my speech on the budget. In 1935 over 23 per cent of our total tax revenues-and after all, the tax revenue comes out of all the people of Canada- were direct. The rest were indirect, or 77 per cent. Today 62 per cent of the federal government tax revenues are from direct taxes. So we have advanced into the field of direct taxation more and more; and as we are able to increase income tax exemptions, for example, those members of the opposition can quote all the more alarming examples by taking people over or under income tax, in which case they pay one hundred per cent indirect say in the low field; but I think the 55704-126i
Excise Tax Act
national average has shown the direction towards direct taxation which this government is following.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar went off the first item onto the sales tax item. I do not know whether I should answer him now, or whether I should preserve an orderly discussion and keep my reply until we reach paragraph 9. He mentioned, for example, that perhaps there are many foods which are not now exempt from sales tax. Well, if he will read schedule III of the Excise Tax Act he will have some difficulty in finding any food purchased by the ordinary householder of Canada-
I was speaking in the past tense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Even in the best example he used he made a fairly understandable error. He talked about the item as of preserved fruits. Actually, preserves in the ordinary sense used by the family have been exempt for many years. Preserved fruit made in the Okanagan valley out of Zuka melons used as fruit filling for cakes for example. They are not candied fruits, and certainly are not preserves, and this item is applicable to that very small field.
So far as salad oils and cooking oils are concerned the hon. member was quite right in pointing out why this has been done. Formerly, and not so long ago, the household used solid fats such as lard and shortening, and the restaurants used cooking oils. Today the housewives also have gone into the use of cooking oils and liquids rather than solids. This is now recognized by the item in the sales tax resolution, paragraph 9.
That would include margarine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member has not given this the study he usually gives these things, for as far as margarine is concerned I think it is the only basic food in Canada which does pay a 10 per cent sales tax. However, I do not intend on this resolution to be provoked into a discussion of margarine.
Margarine is a product of a certain cooking oil which is imported into this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
These are cooking oils and salad oils. Margarine as a manufacturer's product is not an oil. It is actually in solid form and is taxable at 10 per cent sales tax under the federal government's Excise Tax Act.
As far as these drinks are concerned, we have had a most interesting discussion in

Excise Tax Act
past years. There were certain prepared drinks which were made out of fresh milk. Those were exempt because milk always has been exempt, as have eggs. Some manufacturers were going into the business of canning or bottling these drinks and it was contended that they too should be exempt, and this was done. The manufacturers were also making other drinks out of dried milk and dried eggs and they also contended that their products should not be taxed, and we have agreed now to this.
The hon. member probably has the schedule to the Excise Tax Act before him and he will see that the only foods, if you can call them foods, still under the schedule subject to sales tax are various fancy relishes, pickles and things like that. A continuous pressure is being exerted to have them too exempt.
The hon. member commented on baling wire. I think the decision this year is as a result of the discussion last year when several hon. members from the prairies pointed out the inconsistency of exempting baling twine and not baling wire. Not so many years ago only baling twine was used and it is only recently that baling wire has been used to any national extent. Now that hon. members have drawn the attention of the government to the fact that this is a necessary agricultural product, it is included.
The hon. member for Peace River again brought up this interesting question of the incidence of the indirect taxes when applied at the manufacturing level. Perhaps I have had some little effect on him because he seems to remember one major point I brought up and perhaps one minor one. Undoubtedly a tax imposed at the manufacturing level is the easiest and cheapest to collect. There are comparatively few manufacturers. Their sales are not generally made for cash but rather by invoice and there is an accurate record of their sales. The cost of collecting a tax is always important because it would be ridiculous to have a tax when the cost of collection was excessive.
Are the manufacturers paid for making the deduction at the source?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No. The second point was with regard to public acceptance. The hon. member contended that if the public realized that the tax was being imposed they would be more hostile. That is not borne out by the experience of my own province. When the province first imposed a direct sales tax there was great resentment, but when I go home now I am always amazed to see how readily the people pay it. They realize that the tax is put to a good use of which they approve. There is perhaps a third

reason why the federal government has not since the war intervened in the indirect field at the retail level. If the provinces are to have a sales tax they are restricted to a tax at that level.
The other point, which is a matter of considerable importance as far as the efficacy of collection is concerned, is that manufacturers generally make only the one type of goods. That is, a manufacturer would manufacture an article which is either taxable or not taxable. On the other hand, the little retailer handles dozens of articles, some subject to sales tax, some subject to excise tax and others subject to no tax at all. There would be a real accounting job forced on that man if he had to collect tax on his sales, and also the opportunity for evasion would be considerable. It has been a great problem for the provincial administrations which have sales taxes with exemptions.
Some of the states in the United States have found it better to do away with exemptions entirely, to impose a turnover tax of a certain percentage. But that immediately would give rise to members of parliament or members of the legislatures asking for the removal of that tax on food or other things and soon you would be converting from a straight turnover tax to a sales tax.
Then there is the matter of drugs. The minister and his budget committee have given further consideration to extending the list of drugs to be exempted. As was pointed out earlier in this debate some years ago the 5 per cent average medical deduction was reduced to 4 per cent in order to cover the cost of drugs. Consideration has been given to the type of drug which is expensive and in fairly wide national demand, the type of drug which is not used so much for the cure of a disease as for its continual treatment. I suppose insulin is the best example.
The minister has examined the various representations which have been made. Naturally neither the minister nor his budget committee are medical experts and they must rely to a great extent on the advice of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Canadian Medical Association, who after all are the ones who are using these drugs for their patients across Canada. Some of the recent drugs which have been suggested for exemption include substitute blood plasma, aureomycin and streptomycin, and vitamins of high concentration. The minister is giving continual study to these requests and as the opportunity offers the list of drug exemptions is extended.

A few moments ago the parliamentary assistant introduced a new matter

when he said that oleomargarine was the only foodstuff that pays the 10 per cent sales tax. How much per pound is paid on oleomargarine in the way of sales tax? By asking that question I hope to find out what I have never been able to find out, the cost of a pound of margarine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Obviously I have not those figures before me because margarine does not come within the scope of this resolution. I am informed that the actual tax on margarine is around three cents per pound. It varies as the price varies. Once again may I say that that subject is not covered by the resolution. I shall be glad to answer any questions that are within the scope of the resolution.

At three cents per pound that would be placing the cost of the manufactured article at about 27 or 28 cents, which is ridiculous as we know. However, that is not what I want to speak about at the present time. The excise tax on furs and articles manufactured of fur has been reduced from 25 to 15 per cent. When this tax was imposed they imposed it on the raw article. Then another tax is imposed on the processed article, and then there is the sales tax besides.
A farmer finds that he has to pay a tax of $3 on an article which cost him $20 to raise, and that leaves his return at $17 for the raw article. When it is processed another tax is imposed on the tax already paid. These taxes are pyramided and taxed over again. As I have said on several occasions, the trouble is that those who imposed this tax had no idea what they were taxing. But they still continue using the same method and tax this article twice when other articles are not taxed in the same way. They tax it in the raw state, in the processed state and then as a finished garment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot quite understand the hon. member's first point. Schedule III of the Excise Tax Act shows the exemptions from excise tax and at the bottom he will find "furs, raw." I am informed they have been that way for many years.
I know that there is a tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no federal tax on raw furs.
No federal tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no federal tax on raw furs.
I beg to differ with you. If you are correct I should have quite a premium coming back to me. I have already paid it for this season.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would suggest that the hon. member go to the office where he paid it. It
Excise Tax Act
might well be a provincial royalty, which some of the provinces have. So far as the federal Excise Tax Act is concerned, if the hon. member will refer to page 38, schedule III, at the bottom of the page, he will find that raw furs, as are almost all raw products for manufacture in Canada, are exempt from tax. There is of course an excise tax on the processed article. The excise tax which we are now dealing with covers a very wide field of manufactured and processed goods in Canada, but there is no federal tax on raw furs.

Let me try to prove it this way. A farmer has raised a fox and has a silver fox skin. We will say that it costs $20. That is a raw skin. The moment he sells it or offers it for sale to be processed and made into a garment there is a 15 per cent tax applied on that raw article with the result that the purchaser's price is reduced and the farmer only receives $17. I should like to have that explained. I have asked for an explanation on other occasions but it just comes back to the same thing. Surely there is some explanation, or admit that that is so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
All I can read is the law. First of all there is the fact that there is no tax payable on raw furs, which are exempt under schedule III. Then I would refer to page 13 of the office consolidation of the Excise Tax Act. Section 80A reads as follows:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected, an excise tax equal to 25 per cent-
That is now changed to 15 per cent. [DOT]
-of the current market value of all dressed furs, dyed furs and dressed and dyed furs . . .

With respect to the importation of furs, a large quantity of furs is being imported into Canada at the present time. Is there any possibility of having an embargo placed upon Russian furs entering the Canadian market?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is an entirely different matter under the customs tariff resolution. It is not an item of the present resolution. There is a resolution concerning the customs tariff, but according to my recollection it does not include any reference to that.
I shall bring it up later.
I want to ask a question for information. First let me say with respect to the tax on cigarettes that I understand the tax was reduced-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I raise a point? Did we agree to take up the resolution item by item? As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, to dash around from item to item is a little confusing. The cigarette item is well along in the resolution.

Excise Tax Act
I am speaking generally.

Before we finish the general discussion-

On the general question of the sales tax, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and his parliamentary assistant on behalf of my constituents an application they have made that certain articles used by fishermen should be exempt from the sales tax. The general principle that commercial fishermen should benefit by exemption from the sales tax has been on our statutes for some time. At the present time motors for fishing boats, fish nets, fish lines, cordages and barrels for salt fish are exempt. I have had some correspondence with respect to this matter with the Department of Finance, which so far has not produced any success, suggesting that rubber boots, rubber suits, fishermen's work clothes and gasoline and oil
[Mr. Sinclair.
used by commercial fishermen in their fishing operations should also be exempt from the sales tax. The fact is recognized that fishermen's living conditions and income are not any too good particularly in my county where the fish they catch are all processed into smoked and salt fish which are sold at a comparatively low price. I submit if this request were granted it would not make much difference from the point of view of revenue for the department but would mean a lot to the fishermen who have been asking for it insistently and have written to me on several occasions in that connection.
