I want to be in order at all times, but as a matter of information, since margarine was mentioned a moment ago, I should like to know under what item that will come. I sent to my secretary for certain information and she sent me the wrong papers. The information I have entirely discredits the parliamentary assistant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Margarine was only mentioned incidentlly. If any discussion is to be entertained in that regard it would be on paragraph 9. We are now on paragraph 1.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the parliamentary assistant say whether, when this resolution and the section of the bill based thereon are passed, any 25 per cent excise taxes at all will remain?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There will be none at all.

I would like to know whether the companies, say the automobile manufacturers, have reduced their prices to the full

extent of the tax reduction. If the government and members of parliament generally see fit to reduce a tax because of its effect on the buying public, then I think it only fair that this house should make sure that tax reduction is passed on to the consumer.
I do not want to give away any cabinet secrets but my information is that there was an understanding with the government that in the case of some of these tax reductions the full amount of the reduction would be passed on to the consuming public. My observation, together with items I have seen in the newspapers concerning the prices of cars, would lead me to believe that this full tax reduction has not been reflected in the cash price of cars. I would like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether that is so. We should know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the first place the government does not make any agreements with any industries in regard to tax changes. Such changes are first announced in the house after they have been given consideration by the minister and later by the cabinet. The second point is that the government does not set the prices of automobiles.
I did not suggest that you should set the prices of automobiles, but I certainly think you have an obligation to see that tax reductions are reflected in prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would be difficult to do that without setting prices. This matter has been raised in the house; and as hon, members know the representations on this matter for reduction of tax were made partly by the public, partly by the dealers and partly by the manufacturers, who said a reduction in taxation was necessary in order to sell cars. My own feeling from watching the advertisements is that in the light cars, for example, the reduction in advertised prices has been about $150 or $160, which is about 10 per cent of the manufacturers' selling price on such cars. The competition in the automobile business today I think is sufficient safeguard to ensure that manufacturers and dealers will put their products in their showroom windows at the lowest possible prices.

That does not answer the question I asked. I am not mentioning the car dealers or manufacturers to direct any particular criticism at them; I am using them only as an illustration because when I was speaking the other evening the Minister of National Health and Welfare asked me, "What about cars?" According to the article to which I was referring on that occasion, speaking from memory the price of a $2,300 car had been reduced by $140. On the basis of that clipping, which I later sent over to
Excise Tax Act
the minister on his suggestion, the tax reduction of $140 had been based on the price of $2,300, and certainly that is not a 10 per cent reduction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member knows, of course, that the 10 per cent is on the selling price at the factory.

That is right; and as the
Minister of National Health and Welfare and I were sitting at his desk discussing this newspaper clipping we came to the conclusion that the price indicated was the manufacturer's price. That is the point I want to make. In the interests of the country I do hot think we should reduce a tax and then have a company, I do not care whether it is a manufacturer of automobiles or anything else, make a profit on that tax reduction. I believe any reductions should be passed on to the consuming public in full, and I think the government has both a moral and a legal obligation to see that this is done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not here to defend the automobile industry or the car dealers-
I want it understood that I am not trying to criticize the automobile industry as such.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Most of us who understand that the tax is paid on the manufacturers' selling price realize that the reductions have been pretty well in line with the 10 per cent reduction in tax. However, I might point out a fact which has not been given very much publicity. Individual dealers who had cars on hand have suffered quite a loss because of this reduction in tax. They have not publicly complained about it; but when they acquire a car from one manufacturer they pay the tax, and the cars they had on hand on April 8 were cars on which they had paid a tax of 25 per cent. Far from trying to squeeze the public I think the car dealers of Canada, in giving these reductions immediately, showed they were willing to pass along these reductions despite the fact that they had paid the higher tax on those cars they had in stock.

I do not want any misunderstanding in this regard. I can quite understand that a dealer with two or three cars in stock at that time might have taken a loss; but this tax is not applicable to just one or two cars, or one or two cans of tobacco a dealer may have had on his shelf. This is a process which is going to continue for quite a long time, and the parliamentary assistant should not try to suggest that it only affects one or two cars. It will affect every car a dealer gets for perhaps a year or more.

Excise Tax Act

In my part of British Columbia the dealers passed the reduction on to the public. That was stated in half a dozen different newspapers, and the dealers were commended on having done so and given the public a square deal. Of course the dealers out there are not chisellers; they do what is in the public interest.
I thought I heard the parliamentary assistant say there had been no complaints from dealers who had been caught with more than the usual stock of cars on hand when this tax change took place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said there had been no public complaints. Of course the dealers made representations, but they have not been crying to high heaven in the press that they were caught with these cars on hand. The next morning they offered reductions.

In the northern part of western Canada where the harvest was not completed last year many dealers were caught with very large stocks of 1951 cars they were unable to sell. Then the budget came along this spring, before the crop was harvested, and there was a reduction of 10 per cent. Many of those dealers are in rather serious difficulties. Because of the late harvest last year they were unable to sell their stock, and they have had to take a loss on the 1951 cars together with the budget reduction of 10 per cent, which means that on many of those cars they will lose from $300 to $500. I have had letters in regard to this matter from a number of dealers, and have forwarded them to the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would question just one thing; that is, how they can lose $300 to $500 by this 10 per cent reduction in excise tax.

I said they had that loss when they had to sell a 1951 car in 1952, along with the tax reduction. Of course I am not saying the government is responsible for that, but I am saying they have suffered this loss. It is made greater by the fact that they were unable to dispose of their cars last fall and had them on hand this spring when the tax was reduced. The loss is much greater than it would have been in an ordinary year, and therefore this has been a serious matter for them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When the automobile people made their representations to the government prior to the date of the budget, asking that consideration be given to reducing the excise tax, I believe they also made representations with respect to the level at which the tax is applied. I know the parliamentary assistant has already discussed this matter in general terms in reply to the remarks of the

hon. member for Peace River earlier this afternoon, but I should be glad to hear from him any words he may care to offer in connection with this practice as applied specifically to automobiles.
I raise it in this connection for one or two reasons which I shall indicate. I understand that the tax is imposed at the manufacturers' level. That means, so I am told, that many if not all dealers throughout the country, when they take cars into stock, have to pay the excise tax in advance, even though those cars may be held for some time. The results of that are at least two. One is the result that the member for Peace River and others have referred to from time to time, namely the pyramiding of the cost to the eventual consumer. The other is the amount of money which dealers-and they are not all big fellows-may have to tie up in the form of these excise tax payments which they must make in advance.
I understand that some representations were made by the automobile dealers requesting that a change be made in that respect. They asked that the tax be not levied until the actual sale of the hew car is made by the dealer. These people point out that the argument that the parliamentary assistant used today about it being difficult to apply these taxes generally at the last point because of the wide variety of goods and services that are sold in a country like ours hardly applies to automobiles. The automobile is a fairly substantial piece of machinery; every car is well registered, and automobiles do not go astray as public property does sometimes. In that case it should be quite feasible to apply the tax at the point where the car is sold by the dealer to the final purchaser.
One of the reasons that I should like to see it done is to see what the result would be in terms of advantage to the dealers and advantage to the final consumer. I think it would be of advantage to both. It would be a help to the dealers in not having to tie up in advance that money which is simply money paid to the government. It should result also in a lower price for the car to the consumer if the tax does not appear until that final stage. I wonder whether any consideration was given to that specific request from the automobile dealers with reference to this tax on automobiles.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This problem is not unique with automobile dealers. It may be a little more striking, but it does not affect the automobile dealer any more than the dealer, for example, in electrical appliances. A dealer in electrical appliances may have $50,000 worth

of stock in his store on which exactly the same excise tax has been paid at the manufacturers' level. He has had to finance that extra carrying charge in exactly the same way. It looks a little more striking in the case of the automobile dealer because he had fewer units, but I am quite sure the aggregate of a big appliance store as against an ordinary automobile dealer is about the same.
It gets back to the basic problem of whether the tax is to be levied at the manufacturers' level, where it is easily controllable and easily collected, or at the retail level. The first break in the principle, of course, would immediately result in demands from the next largest group of appliance dealers, and so on all the way down. Actually the problem of financing the price paid to the manufacturer is always with the retailers, and that price has always included not only the selling price of the manufacturers but whatever federal or local taxes may be embedded in it. So far as the automobile trade is concerned, because of the very great difficulty some of them had experienced in recent months, they have become highly competitive. The pyramiding to which reference has been made may occur when it is a seller's market, when the dealers can sell anything they get and when, by rule of thumb, they put on 25 per cent or 50 per cent mark-up on anything they buy. Once selling becomes competitive however, and it certainly has been in the automobile field and the appliance field in the last six months, then the dealer can no longer operate in that manner. The retailer has to consider the value of any trade-in; he is aware of the actual mark-up he is getting and sets his price accordingly.
I could not ask for any better evidence of that than from the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones), who must have had a very vivid experience in the last six months in pricing in that field.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There are two comments I want to make. First, I think it would obviously require a great many more electric irons to be in stock to equal $50,000 than it would in the case of automobiles, if the hypothetical example of the parliamentary assistant is used. The other thing I wish to say is that the main argument the parliamentary assistant uses against making this change is that if this break were made and it were done for one group, in due course he would probably have to do it for others. I do not see that it is an argument against taking a step in the right direction to say that you may have to take further steps in that same direction later. Despite the satisfaction of the parliamentary assistant that he has answered this question 55704-127
Excise Tax Act
on former occasions and has answered it again today, I do not feel that he has yet dealt with it satisfactorily so far as we are concerned. Our contention is that by imposing these taxes at the manufacturers' level, it is necessary for the dealers to finance them and this policy does lend itself to pyramiding so far as the consumer is concerned.

If I may follow the hon. member, I should like to emphasize one point that the parliamentary assistant overlooked. He speaks of a retailer having $50,000 worth of electrical appliances, and that is true. It would, however, be a fairly large retailer, whereas throughout the country you find a good many small automobile dealers in the smaller places who might have $50,000 worth of automobiles which they are pledged to sell. In other words, many of the automobile dealers are small people in the sense of having capital, whereas any electrical dealer with $50,000 worth of stock would be fairly large and have a fairly large amount of capital.
The whole problem, as I see it, is that automobile dealers who perform a useful service in the smaller communities in servicing automobiles are often people with a relatively small amount of capital, and the imposition of this tax at the level where it is now imposed does make it difficult for them to finance; that is the whole argument. It is not that we want to extend this principle, but you have a group of people who are in a peculiar position in relation to their capital assets and their ability to pay this particular tax, and at the same time perform a service that is necessary in the community. I think that is the plea that has been made.

I have a question which is somewhat similar. I am told that taxes were collected on cars held by dealers on consignment. My understanding is that the tax is payable when a sale takes place. I take it when a car is on consignment no sale has taken place-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The member raises a case which I remember of one of the larger automobile concerns in Canada who, anticipating perhaps some reduction in taxes, sent the cars to their dealers on consignment for a month before the budget. They said that because of that they had not made a sale to the dealer and there was no need to pay the tax until an actual sale had been made. The Department of Justice ruled that under the actual wording of the act the tax was payable at the time of delivery by the manufacturer, so taxes have been assessed on those cars just as on the cars from other automobile firms which were sent forward in the old way.

Excise Tax Act
May I ask the parliamentary assistant this question? Does the provincial government pay this excise tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You mean the provincial government buying cars? For example, on their cars?
No; buying equipment. Never mind buying cars.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It will depend.
On their road equipment, their snow equipment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is exempt.
The parliamentary assistant says that is exempt?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
If the provincial government is exempt, why is not municipal government exempt?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On my notes here I have the hon. member's name marked down because he raised this problem last year and the arguments against this are the same as those which I advanced last year. We have had the discussions almost every year on that subject. The extension of the right of exemption from excise tax and sales tax to the provincial government is as old as the sales tax. The municipalities are creations of the provincial government. The reasons that I advanced last year still apply. The government has reviewed the situation and has decided that the exemption should be extended only to the provincial governments.

I want to come back to my question. I am a great believer in people paying their taxes, but one runs into cases where governments seem to be-what shall I say-without conscience in the matter of taxes. Today things are being done which in ordinary dealings between individuals would be regarded as intolerable.
I know there is a law to be kept. I know that the parliamentary assistant said that the argument of the Department of Justice is that the tax became payable on delivery, apparently regardless of sale. It seems a curious point, but I am not going to set myself up in argument with the Department of Justice. The question I want to ask is this. Were there distinctions? Were there cases where cars had been delivered on consignment, let us say under legal circumstances A, where they were not regarded as taxable and in other cases where, under legal circumstances B, owing to some slight difference no doubt in the agreement, it was held that they were not taxable on the ground, I presume, that delivery had not taken place?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would prefer to give a full answer to this question when the excise tax bill is actually before us; but the information I have at the moment is that some companies actually rented warehouse space, moved cars from their factories into those warehouses without consignment to any dealer, and actually held the cars themselves; in other words, they distributed them around in order to get them away from the factory. I am informed-but I would want to check that information and give the exact details when the bill is before us-that the tax was not payable; that is, that the 25 per cent tax was not payable on those cars. However, I will give the exact details as to the number of cars involved, if any, when the bill is before us next week.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is discussion concluded on paragraph 1?
I have one question, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry I was not here for all of the discussion. What was the tax before 1951 on these items? Was it all 15 per cent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was not quite all the same. It was 15 per cent on most but it was 30 per cent on soft drinks, candy, chocolate and chewing gum. We are now back to the 1950 status, with the improvement that the 30 per cent tax on confectionery is now also 15 per cent.
On luggage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
What was the tax on luggage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was 15 per cent then. In 1947-48, of course, or up to 1948 we had a 35 per cent luxury tax, a war tax. That was removed in 1948 or 1949. But actually, before these increases were made the excise tax was 15 per cent across the board, with the exception of soft drinks, chocolates, chewing gum and candy where it was 30 per cent. Now it is all 15 per cent.

This will make it possible for the manufacturer to pack his tobacco in any size package he wishes with the knowledge that he will pay tax on that tobacco pro rata at the rate of 80 cents per pound. That has to do with all manufactured tobacco other than cigarettes, such as chewing, smoking and cut tobacco. Paragraph 8 deals with raw tobacco, the leaf tobacco which is not further manufactured into plugs, or cut, or made into cigarettes. The reduction in tax is given as an incentive to grow more of this class of tobacco.
This raw leaf tobacco is just as it is produced by the farmer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

I take it
paragraph 7 includes plug tobacco and refined tobacco for making cigarettes. That tobacco has a higher price than plug tobacco in the trade, without any tax being levied on it. It costs more to produce, does it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I cannot say as far as the
actual cost of manufacture is concerned. In these tobacco taxes we are not concerned with the ad valorem value; it is a specific tax of so much a pound. Whether they make it into plugs or into fine cut for rolling cigarettes or into chewing tobacco, the tax is 80 cents a pound. If the cost of making chewing

Excise Tax Act
tobacco is less than the cost of making fine cut, then of course the cost to the consumer will be less; but that is a manufacturing problem.

But the tax
is the same?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

Do I understand that the change was made in paragraph 7 because you could not work out the tax on let us say an ounce and a half if the rate was 5 cents an ounce; that you had to make it 80 cents a pound so the tax could be worked out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The previous system actually penalized manufacturers for packing their tobacco in other than even ounces. Apparently there are good reasons in the trade why they do not want to pack tobacco in two ounce, four ounce or eight ounce packages. Under the law as it was, you paid 5 cents an ounce or fraction thereof, so if you chose to have a package weighing five and one-third ounces you did not pay tax for five and one-third ounces but for six ounces. You paid for the five ounces and had to pay for a full ounce on the one third. Today you will pay one third of 80 cents.
Why could you not have said "at the rate of 5 cents an ounce"? Would that not have done the same thing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: At the rate of 5 cents an ounce or 80 cents a pound makes no difference. We are removing a penalty under the old wording.
I see that.
I understand, then, that the Imperial Tobacco Company will have to pay tax on the tobacco in bond, then another tax on that when it is processed into cigarettes and then a tax on the cigarettes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; there is one part of this country where the people buy this raw tobacco and smoke it without the necessity of Imperial Tobacco or any other company manufacturing it. On that we get a tax under paragraph 8. So far as the tax on manufactured tobacco is concerned, the excise tax, that is paid by the manufacturer on his manufactured product. The farmer who sells to the manufacturer does not pay that tax at that level, so there is no pyramiding of the tax in that way. This tobacco covered by paragraph 8 is tobacco which is not later manufactured so there is no manufacturing level at which we can recover taxes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall pass on to paragraph 9 which repeals the sales tax on a number of items. Perhaps hon. members could limit their discussion to the items contained in subparagraphs (a) to Oh).
On paragraph 9-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could we not, first of all, have a general discussion on the sales tax? I think perhaps the member for Fraser Valley would agree to that proposal.
It was my understanding from the parliamentary assistant himself that we should follow this procedure, but if I am out of order I shall wait until later.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before we began discussion of this resolution paragraph by paragraph I understood that it had been suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that we were going to have a general discussion on the resolution, and that took place. I thought therefore that, following what we have been doing since the first paragraphs have been discussed, we might analyse each subparagraph seriatim if that is agreeable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was not asking that we should have a broad general discussion such as we had when we were on the first paragraph, but I am suggesting we might at this point have a discussion on the general principle of the sales tax before you ask us to confine our remarks to these particular items.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To follow the wish of the hon. member, if he is to observe the rules, his general discussion of the sales tax would have to be restricted to the particular items mentioned here. He could discuss, generally, that the sales tax is being repealed on the items mentioned in subparagraphs (a) to Oh).

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think the chairman should permit me to welcome the repeal of the sales tax on some items, and to express the hope that it might be repealed on some others as well. The parliamentary assistant has already indicated that there are a few items in connection with which the minister is considering whether or not the tax might be repealed. As a matter of fact, I wanted- I see the chairman is nodding his head.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That, of course, would be a reference in passing.
May I not have a word in this?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I shall be glad to yield to the hon. member and make my remarks later.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member wishes to speak on the matter of procedure we are now discussing.

I am not speaking on the point of order, Mr. Chairman. When I got up some time ago I bowed to the fact that I was possibly out of order, and would wait until another section was called. I represent a dairy district and am therefore interested in this paragraph 9 (a), drinks prepared from milk or eggs. In some areas ice cream is being produced from imported foreign oils. I should like to know from the parliamentary assistant what steps are being taken to protect the people of Canada.
I have a parliamentary return-which is certainly not anything I made up-and it shows that since 1948 approximately 735,450,612 pounds of soya beans have been brought in and manufactured. Some of this material has gone to make the drinks mentioned in paragraph 9 (a). In a return tabled for the member for Lanark it is shown that since 1948,	239,607,700 pounds of copra were
brought in duty free, and that was not mentioned in the previous return. Among other things, this material was manufactured into drinks prepared from milk or eggs. I know that the word "margarine" is almost as repulsive to the parliamentary assistant as it is to me, although from a different angle. I am leaving margarine out of this discussion, because no one would accuse a person of drinking margarine. Milk drinks are definitely being made from these imported oils, and are being sold in Canada. Under a ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada, margarine is also being made and some provinces are even colouring it. The same ruling of the supreme court permits the manufacture of ice cream or these milk drinks out of imported oils.
I should like the parliamentary assistant to tell me just how much the revenues of the Dominion of Canada will be affected by the repeal of the sales tax on drinks prepared from milk or eggs. Obviously it will affect the revenue of every farmer within the dominion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This item, of course, is a further help to the dairy industry of Canada. You will recall that two or three years ago when ice cream was classed as a confectionery we had strong representations, from every corner of the house and especially from members representing farm constituencies, that ice cream be no longer classed as a confection but rather as a food. It was pointed out that would be of assistance to the dairy farmers, and because of that two years ago ice cream was included in the schedule of exemptions from sales tax.
Last year, further representations were made that there were many wholesome drinks made from milk which should get preferential
Excise Tax Act
treatment over other drinks that are not fresh products. We therefore exempted from sales tax preparations made from fresh milk. It has since been pointed out by people who are interested in dairy products that other good manufactured drinks are made out of powdered milk or skim milk and eggs, which are also dairy products. The Minister of Finance has therefore made this further extension of the exemption from sales tax to those drinks which are made from milk or eggs. If these drinks are made from substitutes for milk or eggs such as soya bean oil, to which the member referred, then they are not in this classification and are not exempt from the tax but would pay the sales tax of 10 per cent.

May I say a supplementary word? I think that is a fair explanation that we have had from the parliamentary assistant. It is clear in my mind and I hope it is to the press of Canada and to all the producers of Canada that they cannot in the future use this imported copra or soy bean oil to manufacture drinks as they are doing today and as they have been doing for the last six months.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I want to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that it is no such thing. I said that drinks which are manufactured from milk and eggs are now going to be exempt from sales tax. Drinks which are manufactured from other things-soft drinks, for example -are going .to bear a 15 per cent excise tax as well as sales tax. Other drinks prepared from other materials will come under the usual sales tax of 10 per cent. The only assertion I have made now is that drinks prepared either from fresh milk, dried, powdered or skim milk, or eggs are now totally exempt from sales tax.

I understood the parliamentary assistant to say this. He clearly stated powdered milk and so on, and I accept that statement. But he has also implied, if not stated, that these copra and soy bean oils imported duty free will no longer be permitted in use without taxation-that is sales tax-in milk drinks or in other milk products. He definitely stated that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They always have paid sales tax.
I want to ask this question. This includes liquid and powdered drinks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; drinks.
This is put in the liquid form?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is right.

Excise Tax Act
Then the tax will still remain on the powdered form of drinks?
On such things as Vi-Tone?
Or Ovaltine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: First of all, Ovaltine is not a drink. It is only a drink when it is mixed with water or milk. In the second place those are preparations not solely prepared from milk and eggs.
This tax still remains on powdered drinks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

I have just one word to say. I want to support the hon. member for Peace River in regretting that more drugs have not been placed on the exempt list, particularly vitamin E. I do not want to labour the point because the hon. member for Peace River has dealt with it well in the past and today. I just want to say that I am in full support of what he has said.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with my leader that the hon. member for Peace River has done an excellent job in pressing this point with respect to vitamin E and some other drugs as well. I also feel that further consideration should be given to the whole question of the sales tax and other forms of taxation on drugs and medicines generally. A while ago I put on the order paper some questions with respect to this matter, and I received the answers the day after the budget was brought down. They are to be found at pages 1936, 1937 and 1938 of Hansard for April 9, 1952. I asked these questions:
1.	What drugs and medicines are subject to import duty?
2.	What is the rate of duty on these drugs and medicines?
3.	What other taxes are drugs and medicines subject to, and what are the rates of such other taxes?
It took about two and a half pages to give the details of the duties on drugs and medicines. I will not say anything more about that matter at this point. I will raise that question again when we get to the customs tariff resolutions. I just want to mention in passing that, in addition to the sales tax that applies on drugs and medicines, a good many of them are subject to customs tariffs of various rates.
With regard to question No. 3 which I just quoted, this was the answer given, and of course it corresponds to what the parliamentary assistant said earlier this afternoon:
Sales tax of 10 per cent on drugs and medicines except ACTH; cortisone; insulin; liver extract for use exclusively in the treatment of anaemia.
I believe the parliamentary assistant named one other substance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Radium.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes; he mentioned radium. The four that are listed in the answer that I have just given correspond, of course, to the drugs which are allowed as medical expenses when one computes his personal income tax, provided you get above that 4 per cent floor. We are glad to know that this principle has been recognized as far as it has. But I submit that there are a great many other drugs-not only vitamin E and highly concentrated vitamins-which for the sake of health people are called upon to purchase and to use over a long and continuing period of time. They are almost in the class of food, in the sense that people are required to make use of them. I feel strongly that the sales tax should be removed from those products.
We have in the house two or three druggists, one of whom I see to my right; I refer to the hon. member for Oxford. No doubt they are interested because they are druggists. I was not thinking of that, however. They will know the truth of what I am saying. Although there are perhaps many patented medicines on their shelves on which taxation is not out of the way, they will know that there are many products, vitamins and various other items, that are really essential and which should not be taxed in this way. As I say, the answers given to my questions on April 9 indicate a form of double taxation on a good many of these drugs if they have to be imported into Canada from some other country.
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that there are a number of questions here that all tie in together, I hope you will not think I am out of order if I just mention these in passing in order to indicate how broad this field is. The question that we will be debating at another point, namely, the 4 per cent floor under medical expenses, is related to this matter. The whole question of health insurance is related to it. My feeling is that this government has moved far too slowly in the field of enabling the people of Canada to do something that will help with regard to medical expenses of one kind or another. I think it is a minimum request that we are making when we ask that there should not be this heavy taxation on drugs and medicines.
I just want to ask the minister what things are enumerated in customs tariff 411a, 437 and 476b.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would you mind if we first called (a), (b) and (c)? When we get to them I will give the answer. Would the hon. member mind waiting until we get to (h)? I will read off the whole thing then. We are at (a) now.
Oh, I understand. I thought we were on the clause as a whole.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on (a)?
Carried.
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant why no consideration was given to taking the excise tax off the powdered preparations. It was only put on last year or the year before.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, no;-
It has only been on a short time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -this is not excise tax. This is sales tax.
Sales tax, I should say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It has always been on.
And it is going to continue?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not on powdered milk.
I know it is not on powdered milk. But as to a preparation like Ovaltine, it is made of milk and eggs, and milk has to be added in order to use it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The same sort of answer as that given with regard to soft drinks, candy, chocolate and what not, applies to Ovaltine. Tea and coffee are fairly heavily taxed, and the 10 per cent sales tax does not seem out of line by way of comparison in the same field. As you have seen in the years you have been here, this field of food exemption has been steadily extended until now only specialty foods such as that and various relishes and pickles are not now exempt from sales tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass on to (b) of paragraph 9?
What does this include? Is that for soda fountain purposes or all preserved fruits?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: These preserved fruits are a very narrow class; ordinary preserves, jams, jellies and preserves are already included. There is quite a developing industry of making fruits for baking which are not candied fruits; the Zuka melons of the Okanagan valley are used principally for that. They do not come under the classification of candied fruits, but do not class as home preserves. They were subject to sales tax. They have now been relieved of sales tax.

Would that include cocktail cherries?
Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would include cocktail cherries, if they were not a candied maraschino. A lot of cocktail cherries are made out of these melons. If it were a candied cherry -most of them are-it would not qualify. The bakers use these preserves a great deal for making their cakes.
Where is your explanation of just what preserved fruits means in this instance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the interpretation of the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass on to (c)?
Before we pass on, I believe that someone ought to say something about what I am going to say now.
Are you going to take forty minutes to say it?

We will wait and see. I believe there is altogether too much of a tendency for people in the cabinet, and even members of parliament, to live in a sort of ivory tower. I do not believe that a man like the parliamentary assistant-I have a lot of admiration for him-begins to realize the degree of suffering and privation which is being endured by the common man and his wife throughout the country generally. The income tax and other taxes are so severe, the municipal taxes are so severe, and then the sales taxes are so severe, that if any one of them has a mishap in his family it becomes almost utterly impossible for him to carry on.
It is still better than Russia.
That is no credit to us. Perhaps the hon. member wants us to be like that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do hope that the hon. member will soon give consideration to paragraph (c), cooking oils and salad oils but not including mayonnaise or salad dressing.
I cannot hear what you say, Mr. Chairman, there are so many people trying to talk.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We had a discussion as to the procedure and it was agreed-
I still cannot hear you, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry; I will try to make myself understood. At the beginning of our consideration of these resolutions we had a discussion on procedure. It was agreed that we would limit ourselves to a study of these resolutions paragraph by paragraph. We have proceeded along those lines, and we have already considered all the paragraphs

Excise Tax Act
except paragraph number 9. We have now arrived at a discussion of the subparagraph on sales tax. We have considered the subparagraph on drinks prepared from milk or eggs and also the one on preserved fruits. We are now discussing cooking oils and salad oils but not including mayonnaise or salad dressing. The hon. member may speak.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I was going to say that taxes on absolute necessities, such as certain drugs that mean life or death, are just simply close to criminal. One or two people have written to me concerning their situation. They have simply had to give up their loved ones to die because they could not possibly afford to bring in needed drugs to keep them alive. The drugs are available; they are just across the line. If the taxes were removed they would have a much better chance of getting them; but these taxes, as I have said, are becoming positively criminal. Someone ought to tell the parliamentary assistant, and I hope he tells the Minister of Finance, that he should not try to laugh off too many of these things. Our Minister of Finance comes in here with a jaunty air as if there was not a care in the world.
Would you like him to look sober?

We would like him to look like a sober man, not like a man who is laughing at a funeral. I hope it is conveyed to the Minister of Finance, that something ought to be done for the great common man throughout this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we move to subparagraph (d), baling wire for baling farm produce?
Have you passed subparagraph (c>?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have just called subparagraph (d). If there is no discussion on this subparagraph, we shall move to subparagraph (e), steel pens for farm animals.

I should like to revert to subparagraph (c). The sales tax is repealed on cooking oils and salads, but not including mayonnaise or salad dressing. Does that include the oils for the manufacture of oleomargarine? Or should it read, but not oils for the manufacture of oleomargarine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This tax of course is put on the manufactured product, when the product is packaged and sold as a cooking oil. I will not use the trade name, there are many of them on the market made out of soybean oil, some animal oils, sunflower seed oil. It refers to an oil used as shortening in cooking. Restaurants have used them for many
[The Chairman.]
years. In recent years housewives are turning more and more to using these cooking oils, instead of the same things solidified into lard or shortening. Because of the change in the housewife's habits we are now including these cooking and salad oils used in the homes. They are now exempt from sales tax.
Is margarine not a solidified oil? Should it not come under this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Margarine as such pays a ten per cent sales tax. Butter is exempt; lard is exempt; shortening is exempt; margarine pays 10 per cent sales tax. Those cooking oils-
Why?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Because it is the law.
That is no answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: These cooking oils are now being included on the same basis as lard and shortening because the housewives are using them in increasing quantities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on this question?
Mr. Chairman-

Six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We were dealing with subparagraph (c) of paragraph 8.

I should like to ask for consent to revert to subparagraph (b) for one moment to bring something to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. Some of us feel strongly about legislating in this, shall I say, condensed manner. In this case just the words "preserved fruits" are used and I understand that the details are set out in regulations. Would the parliamentary assistant seriously consider spelling out in the bill, either by reference to the regulations or in some other way, a provision that would settle any doubts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps it would be easier if I read the whole clause as it will appear in the final act. It will be:
Fruit, fresh, canned, frozen, dried, evaporated, preserved.

It seems to me that the difficulty is in not having a further definition of the words "preserved fruits." I understand that there is a regulation which I presume can be altered from

time to time and I still raise the question whether we should be legislating in this way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The department must accept the terminology generally used by the trade. As far as the people who are dealing in these things are concerned, this category of fruit, fresh, canned, frozen, dried, evaporated, preserved has a quite clear meaning to them. It has a meaning quite separate from that of the housewife in connection with jams, jellies and preserves of that type.
If that is the lull statement then it looks as though I am answered. I was told that there is a regulation, but we can deal with that when the bill is before us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Subparagraph (c). If there is no discussion, subparagraph (d).

This item covers baling wire for baling farm produce. This would be the wire used for baling hay, straw, sawdust, shavings and other such things. I understand that it also includes chicken wire used by farmers. Can the parliamentary assistant state whether I am right?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid you are not. Chicken wire is not generally used for baling purposes. Baling wire is the wire commonly referred to as hay wire which is used for the purposes mentioned by the hon. member. This wire is used instead of the twine which was used in the past.

I think I will have to correct the farming knowledge of the parliamentary assistant when he says that baling wire is something used in place of the baling twine which was used in the past. As a matter of fact, there were only a few machines which used twine. Baling wire has been used extensively for at least fifty years to my knowledge.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am happy to have that correction and perhaps that will satisfy the hon. member for Queens.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Subparagraph (e).

Would this cover pens made of fine steel wire which would be used by farmers who are interested in raising mink? I think it should include this type of wire because furs are being taxed in other places and some consideration should be given to the fur producer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This item would not cover the wire used in making pens to enclose fur animals or poultry, for instance. This is the recognition of a need for greater extension to include newer types of farm equipment.
Excise Tax Act
Last year we had a rather unusual item in connection with milking parlours. That seemed a rather odd thing to members who were not acquainted with farm operations, but it was a perfectly proper development in the dairying industry. These steel pens are sold as a unit. It is not a matter of stringing wire on posts. Requests have been made by farm members of this house and by cattle associations for the inclusion of this item. Last year we included stanchions, feeding troughs and milking parlours and this is another extension of the exemption of articles of farm equipment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Subparagraph (f).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine stated earlier that he appreciated the exemption being applied to preservatives used to remove slime from nets and lines or to increase their life. He asked also that rubber boots and rubber capes used by fishermen should be exempted. That raises a difficult problem in the taxation of commodities, the problem of control. Rubber boots and rubber capes are not used solely by fishermen nor are they sold only through fishing supply houses. They are sold generally for industrial and ordinary use. The manufacturer sells to the wholesalers and suppliers, who then sell them to the fishing supply people and to many other retailers. Because of that administrative problem it has not been possible, despite the hon. member's representations, to include them in the considerable list of fishing supplies which are now exempt from the sales tax.

This item is of great interest to the members from the maritime provinces. For some time I have wondered why preservatives used in the fishing industry were not exempt from sales tax. This matter has been brought to the attention of the department and discussed in the house on different occasions. I had received correspondence from fishermen in the province of New Brunswick, from manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, bringing this matter to my attention. Together with the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, the matter was taken up with the department some time ago. Speaking in the chamber on March 12, I mentioned the fact that pesticides or insecticides used in agriculture were exempt from sales tax. For that reason I would expect that materials used for the same purpose in the fishing industry would receive the same treatment. For the benefit of those who do not have any knowledge about this small item, I might say that coal tar is one product used to a great extent all over the maritime provinces.

Excise Tax Act
We have to contend with the marine borer and in many parts of the maritime provinces lobster pots have to be dipped completely in coal tar. Prior to the war coal tar sold for $5, $6 or $7 a barrel. Since the war it has steadily increased in price until today it costs the fishermen about $22 a barrel, and there was a sales tax of $2.20 added to that retail price. I know this step will be appreciated by those engaged in the fishing industry. Catechu and other preservatives are also used. They would come under this item and that also will be of some benefit to the fishermen. I want to take this opportunity to thank those responsible for giving serious consideration to this problem and finally deciding to do away with the sales tax. I can assure the officials of the department who are responsible that the move will be appreciated by all fishermen of the maritime provinces.

I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Charlotte has just said with respect to this concession to the fishermen of the maritime provinces particularly. At the same time I should like to point out that the hon. member for Charlotte first brought this matter to my attention a couple of years ago. I join with him in expressing the appreciation of the fishermen of our part of the country for the relief given to them under this item. The loss of revenue to the government may not amount to very much but the saving to the fishermen, who felt previously that they could ill afford to pay this tax, is a really big item to them. Again I should like to thank the officials of the department responsible for this relief.

I should also like to say a word about this matter. The fishermen on the bay of Fundy coast engaged in hand lining and that type of fishing are also interested in this matter, and I know that the relief that has been given will be appreciated by them. However, I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant that this is only a beginning on what I think should be further consideration of the problem of the fishermen. After all, the department has gone a long way throughout the years in dealing with the farmer. Today a very large part of the equipment used in the farming industry is exempt from sales tax, and properly so. The fisherman, who is also a primary producer and who is facing very serious problems, should be given more consideration than has been the case heretofore. The parliamentary assistant mentioned a moment ago the problem involved in connection with the goods mentioned by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine. Obviously there are administrative problems but I think they can be overcome. Gasoline used by farmers is coloured

in some way and is not liable for tax. I am quite sure that the manufacturers of fishermen's goods could put a mark on them of some kind so that they could be recognized as such and be exempt from sales tax if such an exemption were granted. Some sort of brand could be put on them, probably not by way of colour but in some other way.
So the miner could not wear them.

I am sure it can be done. It is a matter of working it out. We realize there are administrative details but there are far greater problems confronting the fishing industry today than the problems of administration confronting the department. Can the parliamentary

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

Has the parliamentary
assistant a list of what are termed preservatives for the treating of rope? speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In inquiring about this matter I of course was thinking of the types of preservatives used by the fishermen in my own riding, but I am happy to tell the hon. member that the officials of the department mentioned cutch used in the maritimes and said it was a most excellent preservative with no administrative problems since it apparently has no other use except as a preservative of netting. It is included.
It is a soluble gum.
Not much of a preservative, either.

There is good reason for thanksgiving this evening so far as the items included in this particular paragraph are concerned. On behalf of the fishermen of the constituency I represent-and there are many of them-I want to thank the government and the Department of Finance particularly for the splendid effort they are making to help the fishermen to reduce their costs of production.
Some three years ago I raised the question that was brought up today by the hon. member for Gaspe, not with the finance department especially but with certain members of the government. I was interested in having something done to reduce the sales and other taxes on gasoline used by fishermen. At that time I was given the same explanation the parliamentary assistant has given tonight. Of course I can see great difficulties in the way of doing anything of that kind, though of course it has been done in other industries. I was glad to hear the parliamentary assistant point out that many things have been done to reduce the cost of production of the fishermen, though often these are not well known by some of the smaller fishermen. The parliamentary assistant pointed out that there is a schedule which sets out all the articles on which taxes have been removed. I do not want to delay the committee longer; I rose only for the purpose I indicated.

On behalf of the fishermen of Newfoundland and Labrador I should like to say a word of thanks for this exemption from the sales tax. As other hon. members have said already, I would like to see the government go further and exempt certain other items as well. In regard to rope, for example, I know certain sizes of rope are exempt now from sales tax, but I think the officials of the department might look into
Excise Tax Act
the possibility of having the larger sizes exempt as well. While the smaller sizes of rope are used by the individual fishermen, the larger sizes are used on the vessels in which these fishermen go out to sea.
While I am on my feet I would like to support the request made this afternoon by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine that certain other articles he referred to be exempt in order that the expenses of the fishermen might be reduced and their earnings increased. As I said before, I would like to see this list of exemptions made much larger, in order that these men who gain their livelihood reaping the harvest of the sea may be encouraged by seeing something done to assist them. What section does this come under? Is it under the Excise Tax Act?

How much will the government lose in revenue by removing this tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:

I wonder if the parliamentary assistant could tell me whether this also applies to anhydrous copper sulphate?

What is the customs tariff now on items 411a, 437 and 476b?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The reason we are putting 411a in here is to carry out what has been the administrative practice under a ruling of the tariff appeal board. Item 411a reads: Machinery, logging cars, cranes, blocks and tackle, wire rope, but not including wire rope to be used for guy ropes or in braking logs going down grade, and complete parts of all the foregoing, for use exclusively in the operation of logging, such operation to include the removal of the log from stump to skidway, log dump, or common or other carrier.
That is at present administratively carried out, but we are now putting it in the act.
The second thing is perhaps of more general interest, though I am quite sure that item 411a is of great interest to certain hon. members here. Item 437 covers the following: Locomotives, cars and coaches and repair equipment, belonging to railroads, brought temporarily into Canada for the purpose of clearing obstructions, fighting fires or making emergency repairs on railway lines within Canada;
When railway equipment is brought in here from the United States on rental to Canadian railways, as sometimes occurs, we do charge them sales tax. Occasionally when a disaster occurs, such as a bridge going out or a fire, it is necessary to move in railway equipment through the United States to fix the bridge or fight the fire. The Railway Association has made representations that it was unfair to assess sales tax or the l/60th duty per month on railway apparatus brought in for that purpose.
The item also covers:
. . . detector cars when Imported to test rail in tracks in Canada.
There are new types of cars turned out by the Sperry Company whereby the car itself going down the track can detect a crack in the rails that is not obvious so far as the observation of the track walker is concerned. There are no such cars permanently in Canada, and up to the present time they have come in for testing Canadian lines.
The third item covers:
Surgical suction apparatus including motive power; prepared surgical sutures; ethylene; operating room lights designed to minimize shadow, not including bulbs; all the foregoing of a class or kind not made in Canada, and complete parts thereof, for the use of any public hospital, under regulations prescribed by the minister.
There is one other item which I should mention because it is not covered by the resolution. The customs tariff item and the excise tax items should be generally in the same language, and these items on artificial limbs have been different in the two acts.

Tonight, therefore, in the excise tax resolution and in the customs tariff resolution we are going to make the items the same. We are changing that to read, "artificial limbs, spinal and other orthopedic braces and parts of the foregoing". The same wording will be in the customs tariff resolution to which we shall come later.

Can the parliamentary assistant say whether any consideration has been given to exempting safety equipment which the boys are required to wear in accordance with their duties in the mines?

Is consideration being given to exempting from sales tax materials and goods used in the treatment of cancer? I have been asked about it. I feel it should be exempted, because the material cannot be purchased in Canada at all. These victims have to buy it in large quantities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not familiar with the equipment to which the hon. member is referring. This afternoon I said that recommendations, for the most part, did come from the Department of National Health and Welfare and further back from the medical profession. Excise Tax Act

There is one thing that is in continuing use by the victims of deafness. Did the government give consideration to the exemption from duties and sales tax of equipment for the deaf? If anything is to be done about it, it should be taken into immediate consideration. Has the parliamentary assistant any comment on that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is just a technical question, but when the parliamentary assistant first began to discuss paragraph 9(h) he said that these changes were being made to bring the statutory provisions into line with administrative practice following a decision of the tariff board. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The first point, of course, so far as the tariff board is concerned, is that not only matters in respect of tariff coming under the Department of National Revenue, but also rulings by the department on excise and sales tax matters can be appealed to the tariff appeal board. That is the first

Excise Tax Act
point. The second point was that the appeal was made against the wording in the act. The intent had been carried out by the department. This was the intent that had been carried out. The ruling of the tariff board on the present wording in the act was adverse to that intent. Item 411a has now been changed to carry out what was the practice, what was the intent and what is the wish of the industry as far as that is concerned. But the hon. member's primary point is as to appeal to the tariff board. That board can be appealed to on matters of excise tax or sales tax as well as tariffs.
Before we get too far from the item which I raised, I should like to point out that what the parliamentary assistant was talking about in item 482 was the matter of tariffs. I think he said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.

This particular item on which we are now working is paragraph 9, which reads "That the sales tax on the following goods be repealed." My question had not reference to item 482 in the tariff rates which we shall come to later. What I asked him was whether any consideration has been given to the abolition of the sales tax on those particular goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The reason I mentioned the customs tariff, Mr. Chairman, was that he actually asked me whether anything had been done in that regard. I said that nothing had been done.

I beg the parliamentary assistant's pardon. I did not ask him any such thing. I asked whether the government had given any consideration to the abolition of the sales tax on those particular items, namely equipment for the deaf, such as batteries and so on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: I am talking about the sales tax. I should like to know where that sales tax on such goods is collected. As to this equipment for the deaf which is coming from the United States, where is the sales tax collected?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The sales tax on any import is collected at the place of import.

Exactly; and that is the point. That is the reason why I mentioned that these goods came chiefly from the United States. In my experience-and I have had half a dozen cases of this particular type- the fact is that this sales tax is collected at the border, and the delay is not owing to the tariff or the customs duty but is owing to the collection of the sales tax at the border point. I have known, from my own experience, of a lady who had to wait ten days or two weeks until these formalities were taken care of; in her particular case she could perhaps afford to pay the sales tax. But the point is that the sales tax is collected at the border and it causes delay. That was her particular complaint, and I think her complaint was a valid one. These people are absolutely helpless without their hearing aids; they might as well not be living as far as any association With other people is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the sales tax on goods which are imported is collected by exactly the same officials who collect the customs tariff and the excise tax, if applicable, namely the officers of the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue. I pointed out that consideration has been given, that a measure of relief has been given,-
With regard to the sales tax?

speechtext: -a measure of relief actually more substantial than mere removal of the sales tax, if he will consult the customs tariff.

speechtext: Excise Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall now take up the resolution dealing with the Excise Act which reads as follows:

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Act, 1934 and to provide:
1.	That the duty of excise on spirits distilled from wine produced from native fruits and used in the treatment of domestic wine be repealed.
2.	That the duty of excise on spirits used directly in the manufacture of goods subject to excise tax under schedule I of the Excise Tax Act be repealed.
3.	That the duty of excise on beer or malt liquor brewed in whole or in part from any substance other than malt be reduced from forty-five cents to forty-two cents per gallon.
4.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution be deemed to have come into force on the ninth day of April nineteen hundred and fifty-two.
We shall deal with the paragraphs seriatim. Is there any discussion on paragraph 1?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the parliamentary assistant explain this paragraph? Perhaps he can give a general explanation with regard to this resolution as a whole.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Hon. members may recall that those members who are from the areas of Canada which produce wine, the Niagara peninsula, part of Quebec, the Okanagan valley and Vancouver island, at various times have protested against foreign wines in one respect being more favourably treated as far as taxation is concerned-that is aside from customs tax-than domestic wines. The reason for that lay in the fact that as far as light wines are concerned, wines of ordinary fermentation, Canadian wines have an advantage; but on wines which are called fortified wines, wines to which spirits are added, heavier wines, for example, sherry, to which grape alcohol has been added, the Canadian wines suffer a disadvantage because we levy an excise duty on the spirits which they use to fortify the wine, and when the wine is sold to the public we put an excise tax on it. They objected first of all to the fact that we levied this excise duty on what was an article used in the manufacture of goods. In general we try to avoid that. They objected also to the fact that there was a pyramiding of taxes since the excise tax was then paid on the resulting cost of the wine, which included not only the cost of the spirits to fortify the wine, but the excise duty on it. And the various members from those ridings, the grape growers association and the wine growers associations on many occasions have asked that this problem be considered. It has been, and we are now removing the extra duty of $1.50 a gallon on those spirits which are used in the manufacture of these strong wines to fortify them. We still at the end have the
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
same excise taxes; that is, when the wines are sold to the public, of 50 cents a gallon on still wines, and $2.50 a gallon on sparkling wine.

What is the difference
between light wine and strong wine? What is the difference in alcoholic content? When does a wine become strong wine, and when does it cease being a light wine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My understanding is just at the point when it is fortified; when it has gone through its own process of natural fermentation and then has to be fortified with distilled spirit, ' which is generally a grape brandy, it is a strong wine; that is the wine on which this special excise duty is applied. On the ordinary wine, which is not fortified, this duty of course does not apply. It was only on the wines such as port and sherry, which come to my mind, continental wines which are fortified, that this applied.
Irrespective of the strength of the wine at natural fermentation, it does not come into this category?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Light-
No matter how strong is the alcoholic content of natural wine, it does not come under this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A natural wine does not use spirits for its fortification. I think if you remember your high school chemistry, or perhaps your efforts and mine to make home brew or homemade wine, you will recall that there is an early limit to natural fermentation.
It blew up eventually.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There is little variation
between the strength of natural fermentation of wine and beer. The next step to get it up to 20 per cent alcoholic content can only be reached by the addition of the spirits. I think the hon. member for Lincoln wants to speak on this. He is more of an authority on this matter than you or I.

I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant on the inclusion of this matter in the tax item that we are discussing at this time, because it has to do with a very important industry in the district from which I come, namely, the producing of grapes in the district of the Niagara peninsula. There are many grape growers in the Niagara peninsula, the majority in the constituency of Lincoln and some in the constituency of Welland.
What about Wentworth?

And there are some in Wentworth too. To a great extent, they depend

on the growing of grapes. We appreciate very much the effort that has been made by the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant in arranging to have this tax repealed which we feel is an unjust tax on the grape growers of the Niagara district. It put us in a very unfavourable position with regard to wine which is imported from California, South Africa, South America and other countries. This deletion is only fair treatment for the grape growers and domestic wine producers of the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We shall now discuss
paragraph 2 which deals with the excise tax on spirits used directly in the manufacture of goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I may give a word of explanation on this. These spirits referred to in item 1 are also used in the manufacture of certain mouth washes and hair lotions and things like that, and exactly the same argument applies, namely, that they pay an excise duty when they manufacture it, then they pay an excise tax and a sales tax on the finished product. Since we were clearing up the situation as far as the wine growers were concerned we decided to do the same thing with respect to those other manufactured products.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any discussion on paragraph 3?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am glad to hear the parliamentary assistant admit in what he has said on the first two paragraphs of this resolution that there is such a thing as a tax that pyramids.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Very rare-these cases are so rare-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hon. members are laughing, but they will recall that our two main indirect taxes are sales taxes and excise taxes, and they are not pyramided. They are calculated on the same base. This was one of the rare examples where there was one in the wine. I made a little error with the wine, since the excise tax on wine is specified by the gal-lonage. Therefore it was not pyramided; but in the case of the mouth washes and the hair lotions there was an element of pyramiding because of the application of 10 per cent sales tax to the finished product.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is no discussion on paragraph 3, we shall proceed with paragraph 4.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There is another anomaly in paragraph 3. Ninety-five per cent of the beer in Canada is made from malt, and we tax the malt to secure the tax on the beer pro-
Customs Tariff
duced, and we tax it at the rate of 21 cents a pound. It takes two pounds of malt to make a gallon of beer, and that is at the rate of 42 cents a gallon. There are several other beers in Canada, some made from rice and some made from corn flakes, other than malt, and they have been in the past taxed at 45 cents a gallon. The essence is that here in Canada there are two principal manufacturers of glass, one a branch of a British company and one a branch of a United States company. They make what is commonly called sheet glass; they do not make plate glass. There are considerable imports from Great Britain, the United States, Belgium, France and Czechoslovakia.
When glass is imported for manufacture into other products, such as plate glass and the better qualities of sheet glass for manufacture into mirrors, it was subject to a drawback of 50 per cent. The most important item in the new glass schedule is item 319, which covers plate glass, formerly dutiable under tariff items 320, 321 and 322. Item 320 covered plate glass in sheets up to 7 square feet and was duty free under the British preferential tariff and a most-favoured-nation rate of 10 per cent. Item 321 provided for plate glass in sheets over 7, but not over 25 square feet, duty free under the British preferential tariff with a most-favoured-nation rate of 20 per cent.
I might say in passing that there is no general rate on glass because countries outside the general agreement covering most favoured nations are not exporters of glass, or for that matter manufacturers of glass,
Except Czechoslovakia.
