Item 322 provided for plate glass, n.o.p., at rates of 17-J per cent under the British preferential and 25 per cent under the mostfavoured-nation tariff. A drawback of 99 per cent of the customs duty applied to plate glass when used in the manufacture of safety glass. This provision for a drawback is now being cancelled and plate glass will continue to be duty free under the British preferential tariff with a most-favoured-nation rate of 5 per cent.
The imports of plate glass during 1951 were valued at $6,730,000. The United Kingdom supplied $2,167,000 worth, United States $3,460,000 worth, Belgium $970,000 worth, France $72,000 worth, and Germany $62,000 worth.
The item of second importance in the new glass schedule is item 318, which now covers ordinary window glass and thick window glass. The former item 318 provided for ordinary window glass duty free under the British preferential tariff with a most-favourednation rate of 10 per cent. Item 319 provided for thick window glass duty free under the British preferential tariff with a mostfavoured-nation rate of 20 per cent. A drawback of 50 per cent of the duty was allowed on

The drawback provision is cancelled and window glass continues duty free under the British preferential tariff with a reduction in the most-favoured-nation rate from 10 per cent to 7J per cent. The other important items in the new glass schedule are 322(a), 322(b) and 323, the items covering laminated glass or safety glass. We have had plate glass, sheet glass and now this is the third major glass item in Canadian industry. During 1951 the imports of the glass provided for in these items amounted to only $129,000 worth, but during 1950 the value of the safety glass manufactured in Canada reached almost $10 million. There was $10 million worth made in Canada and $129,000 worth imported. Laminated glass and manufactures thereof were formerly dutiable under tariff item 322a at the rate of 17J per cent under the British preferential tariff and 25 per cent under the mostfavoured-nation tariff. The new item 322(a) reduces the tariff on laminated glass, not further processed than cut into rectangles, to 5 per cent under the British preferential tariff and 124 per cent under the mostfavoured-nation tariff. The former rates of 174 per cent under the British preferential tariff and 25 per cent under the mostfavoured-nation tariff are continued on laminated glass further processed than cut into rectangles and on manufactures of laminated glass. In other words, the semifinished product when imported in sheets without finishing into sizes carries a considerably lower tariff than the finished product when it is brought in exactly in the shape of windshields and so on. Those are the three principal classifications and the three principal items.

I must confess that, in all the study I have done on these resolutions so far, the most baffling has been this report on plastics because the language is completely foreign to that used by anybody in the House of Commons. The tariff board spent a great deal of time on an actual study of the situation. They called in not only the manufacturers of the basic plastic products but also the manufacturers of the secondary products, and this schedule is to their general satisfaction. It carries through the same basic principle of giving a low tariff or no tariff at all on raw materials not of a class or kind manufactured in Canada, with a slight tariff on those which are manufactured in Canada, and intermediate tariff on semi-processed imports, and a higher tariff on finished articles.

The plastics industry is growing very rapidly in Canada today, particularly in the west, in Alberta with the resins and in British Columbia with the cellulose plastics. In the semi-processed stage the rates are higher; and in the finished stage, which Canadian manufacturers should be able to manufacture if not from primary plastics of Canadian manufacture then from plastics imported from Britain or the United States, the rates are still higher. That is the general pattern which rims through this new schedule which now covers both resin and cellulose plastics.

I quite appreciate the problems in connection with the development of the plastic industry, but I think the hon. gentleman will agree that this type of plastic covering will have a very small demand in Canada as a whole. I would think it is a type particularly suitable and necessary for farm use, and I suggest that consideration should be given to its exemption when used on farms. I am quite sure it is not manufactured in Canada at all, or if it is the manufacturing is done in western Canada, which raises problems of freight, deliveries and so on in the east.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That will certainly be given consideration. I fully realize the force of what the parliamentary assistant says about this strange new language we are now speaking, but there are one or two general business considerations which I think are relevant. Can we be informed as to how much of what we use in Canada is currently being imported; how much is made by whom, and who are the chief competitors? with natural gas and oil has given that industry great encouragement. The Columbia cellulose plant in Prince Rupert, which is going to have a chemical plant in Edmonton, is another example of that development. But except by reading the report to the committee in detail, with column after column of figures showing the production of individual companies, I am afraid I cannot give any easy summary.
There is one important point in my opinion, however, which I think should be emphasized. As you know, by the Geneva agreements many of our existing tariff rates have been bound for three years, which means we cannot increase them. Even though we can give reductions to other countries, we cannot increase those rates. Those bindings, of course, were given in return for bindings of value to Canada in other countries; but we were very careful in new fields, where we could not assess the impact of such bindings, not to give any assurances or bindings of that kind. I would like to draw attention to a paragraph in the report of the tariff board which points that out:
The board does not, in this report, recommend rates of duty which will apply when goods not now made in Canada begin to be produced in this country. The board is aware that industry is concerned lest low or free rates on goods not now manufactured in Canada may become bound against increase under international agreement.
They are thinking, of course, of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
In view of the rapidity with which this industry is developing and changing, the board recommends that those responsible for Canada's tariff policy bear this point in mind when undertaking international negotiations or, indeed, when new materials in this field are produced in quantity in Canada.
I may say the Minister of Finance has certainly accepted this recommendation. Moreover the chairman of the tariff board, which made this report, has been on the various Canadian delegations at Havana, Geneva, Annecy and Torquay at which various items were bound, so he is well aware of the problem.

The problem of establishing fair market values for goods from behind the iron curtain is very difficult. That was one of the points raised by the Americans in their denunciation of their trade relations with Czechoslovakia. It is almost impossible for our trade commissioners to circulate freely in Czechoslovakia and find out the current selling prices in that country of the type of goods they send to us. It is even more difficult for individual salesmen going to Czechoslovakia to ascertain those prices. On the other hand it is perfectly open to any Czechoslovakian trade commission or businessman to come to this country and find the fair market price of any commodity. That is undoubtedly a great problem.
However, I think most hon. members are aware that the glass industry was recently the subject of a report by the combines investigation branch. It is an industry in which there is not as much competition as generally exists in other industries in Canada. We have for the most part the Pilkington group of England, who are here with two branch factories, and the Pittsburgh Glass Company of the United States who are here with two or three factories under various names. The only real competition for those two groups comes from those individual Canadian importers who bring in Belgian, French. German and Czechoslovakian glass. Personally I feel that it is pretty healthy to have that competition, especially when you remember that there is only one glass company in all Britain. The Pilkington company is the only glass company there.
I do not want to bring in the findings of the combines branch in connection with the glass industry of Canada, but I feel that the removal of the drawback and the lowering of the duty will be a healthy thing as far as competition in the glass industry in Canada is concerned, and will be of benefit to those who use glass, especially the ordinary household where glass is used for windows and mirrors.

The second item mentions attachments to be combined with automobiles in Canada for use on traction engines and parts thereof. It uses the word attachment there and not the word accessories. I think there is a point here which should be investigated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the discussion of the tariff schedule, a discussion which is almost continuous in the department-because these representations come forward the year round, unlike income tax representations which are generally made just before the budget-I do not know of any item to which more attention has been given than to this tractor item because of the problem raised and because of the wide use of tractors. I am informed that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made such a suggestion. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in putting forward proposals on behalf of the farmers, naturally want all taxes removed from all types of equipment that can be possibly used by farmers, and to a great degree that has been accomplished in recent years; but as far as the administration of the Department of National Revenue is concerned, this is the wording which they want, and in view of their experience this is the wording which will include all bona fide accessories on tractors, but will exclude others.

If there is any regulation which distinguishes between attachments and accessories I should like to know just what the interpretation is as to what is an attachment and what is an accessory. They must have some definition which they go by. I would like to get these two definitions.

I should like to say a word in connection with books, and I am speaking

Customs Tariff
now on item 708a. Certain publications are admitted to Canada free, but I suggest that there are other publications which should be admitted free and which should not be subject to sales tax. I think hon. members will agree that a contact with books generally is the best form of adult education you can have. There is a school of thought among educators and others that we are neglecting to make the works of the literary masters available to our students, even our university students.
We seem to be turning more and more to digests, synopses and extracts, and to my mind those are no substitute for the original book in the hands of the student. I think the main reason for such substitution is the high price of books. As far as the reading public is concerned, and I am afraid this includes the younger reading public, it seems to be turning more and more to trash, the kind of book that is the cheapest. I refer mainly to the 25 cent books to be purchased in drug stores, pool rooms or tobacconists.
I should like to say something with regard to censorship for the benefit of the Minister of National Revenue. I do not intend to commit myself now as being in favour or not in favour of censoring our reading matter, since I should be called to order, but I do want to say that we might as well not have any censorship in this country as to have the type of censorship we have.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to what item he is addressing his remarks.
Item 708a.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That refers to publications of the United Nations.
Perhaps the item should be 696 which refers to items for the use of colleges, academies, schools or seminaries of learning in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The two items are 696 and 708a.
I shall trust to the discretion of the chairman to direct me as to which item is the appropriate one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps I should inform the hon. member that the reason I rose was that I heard him speak about the censorship exercised by the Department of National Revenue. We are dealing now with various items, and if he is dealing with 696 or 708a he may do so but only inasmuch as they have to do with the increase or reduction of tariffs, or whatever treatment they are being given under this resolution.

I shall avoid censorship, Mr. Chairman. I merely want to say that many

of these 25 cent penny dreadfuls can be found among the books which are on the censorship list of Canada. However, I shall say no more about that. With respect to the publication of decent literature we are very far behind Great Britain, for example, in the publishing of cheap editions of good books. Rather than restricting, I think the government should encourage the widest circulation of books and literature of all sorts. The sales tax and the customs duty do raise the prices of books which in my estimation are altogether too high in Canada, and that is one of the reasons why people are forced to read the sort of thing about which I have been talking.
Another point is that Canadian publishing houses, in selling books which they bring in from the United States and upon which they pay duty and brokerage, charge Canadian customers 10 per cent more than the price for which the Canadian customer can purchase the same book from the original publisher in the United States and then pay the customs duty and sales tax himself. These United States exporters find it convenient to set up branches in Canada, and we are in fact subsidizing the establishment of these institutions at the expense of the public and the Canadia university student in particular.
To come back to the tariff, I am aware that on the free list of publications there are, as well as those mentioned in 708a, certain educational books for university libraries or books prescribed for the regular curricula of schools and universities. However, I want to point out that unlike the items in 708a, reference books which are brought in by bona fide professors in universities and teachers in schools for reference purposes are subject to the tariff which is not charged on the publications in this item. I think that is a state of affairs that could very well be altered. If a professor or teacher is worthy of the name he does not confine himself to the textbooks prescribed by the curriculum. He wants reference books, and as long as he is a bona fide university professor or teacher I see no reason why these books should not be admitted free. I shall go further and say that it would be better for the educational standards of the country-and goodness knows education at the moment is in a deplorable state-if educational books of all types were admitted free of not only customs duty but sales tax, for sale not only to people in educational institutions but to the public at large. In my opinion the government should collect no revenue which involves any limitation upon the wide circulation of educational books. Indeed, I think I would go further and say on any books.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should like to speak on this item. Are you going to speak on books?

Yes. I shall be very brief. I had had representations from libraries and others along the general line indicated by the hon. member who has just spoken. Certain public libraries and our parliamentary library, I believe, have to pay not only duty but sales tax on books brought into Canada. I think it is a rather anomalous situation that at least should be considered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have heard so much about this matter in recent years that I think tonight I had better put on the record exactly what the situation is as far as books are concerned. To listen to the hon. member for Saskatoon, one would think there was a heavy tariff on books. Actually there is no tariff at all on any book coming into Canada from within the British commonwealth. I think our first responsibility is to see that there is the freest exchange of books and literature between the various members of the commonwealth. I think it might also be desirable to put on the record the various tariff items as far as books, pamphlets and periodicals are concerned, which those who are really interested in this matter could have easily consulted the customs tariff and ascertained. Tariff item 169 reads as follows:
Books, viz.:-Novels or works of fiction, or literature of a similar character, unbound or paper bound or in sheets, but not to include Christmas annuals, or publications commonly known as juvenile and toy books.
Under the British preferential tariff they are free, most-favoured-nation tariff 10 per cent, and general tariff 25 per cent. Then we have four separate treaties with various other countries to permit the free exchange of books between our country and those countries. Tariff item 170 reads as follows:
Books, periodicals and pamphlets, or parts thereof, printed, bound, unbound, or in sheets (not to include blank account books, copy books, or books to be written or drawn upon (in any other than the English language).
Under the British preferential tariff they are free, most-favoured-nation tariff free, and general tariff free. We also have a reference to the United States trade agreement there. The next tariff item which members could have read is 171. It reads as follows:
Books, printed, periodicals and pamphlets, or parts thereof, not otherwise provided for, not to include blank account books, copy books, or books to be written or drawn upon.
In other words, blank books do not come in under that item but other books not otherwise provided for do. Under the British preferential tariff they are free, most-favourednation tariff 10 per cent, the general tariff 55704-129J
Customs Tariff
10 per cent. Then we have four other trade agreements with special reference to free exchange between these countries and our country. The next item is 171a which reads as follows:
Printed sections of dictionaries and encyclopedias, unbound, consisting of not less than eight uncut pages, when imported by book binders to be bound in cloth or leather in their own factories.
Under the British preference they are free, most-favoured-nation free, and general tariff free. Then we have tariff item 172 which reads as follows:
Books, pamphlets and charts, printed or published by any government abroad; official financial and business reports and statements issued by companies or associations abroad; books, pamphlets and reports, for the promotion of religion, medicine and surgery, the fine arts, law, science, technical training, and the study of languages, not including dictionaries.
We covered those in the previous item. The item continues:
Scripture and prayer cards, and religious pictures and mottos, not to include frames; books, bound or unbound, which have been actually printed and manufactured more than twelve years; manuscripts; insurance maps; freight rates, passenger rates and timetables issued by transportation companies abroad and relating to transportation outside of Canada in book or in pamphlet form.
Under the British preferential tariff they are free, most-favoured-nation tariff free and general tariff free. Tariff item 172a refers to tourist literature from any country and in each case entry is free of duty.
Item 172b:
Prayer books, missals, psalters, religious pictures and mottoes, not to include frames; free, free, free.
Then item 173:
Books which are included in the curriculum of any university, college or school in Canada for use as text books or as works of reference, not to include dictionaries; printed books, pamphlets and cards for use in schools to test the degree of intelligence of pupils; all books for bona fide libraries, and being the property of the organized authorities of such libraries and not in any case the property of individuals or business concerns, under such regulations as may be prescribed by the minister; directories for free reference libraries; books received from free lending libraries abroad, subject to return under customs supervision, within sixty days: free, free, free.
The Minister of Public Works tells me to send the hon. member a copy of the rest of the schedule. Actually, of course, the great bulk of the books imported into Canada come in free. The one substantial class of books on which there are tariffs are novels from the United States, on which the tariff is 10 per cent. I emphasize again that these books for use in colleges, schools and universities, or books coming to bona fide libraries from any country, come in free. Books in foreign languages come in

Customs Tariff
free. All books from the British commonwealth come in free. So the position, far from being that suggested by the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon, is that the tariff actually affects very few publications as far as the importation of books into Canada is concerned.
I am glad the parliamentary assistant has been able to tell me that we have free entry of books into this country. I did not hear what the tariff is on books coming from the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is 10 per cent on novels, nothing on books for schools, universities, libraries.

When my hon. friend says that books for universities come in free it is a bit misleading, because bona fide university professors do not obtain all their books free. I suppose a great many Canadians get or would like to get books from the United States, but on those books they have to pay a customs duty as well as a sales tax.
Perhaps the greatest point the parliamentary assistant made was that there is no need to raise -this question, that books are practically free as far as tariff is concerned. He told us about books from the commonwealth and all the rest of it; he read a long list of things that come in free. The point is that I can base my argument on that very fact. I would say the revenue the Canadian government is getting from the restrictions it is imposing on the importation of books to this country is not worth it. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant could tell me just how much the duty on books is worth to the national revenue of this country. As I interpret his words it would be very little indeed; -and if it is very little indeed I would say it has only nuisance value, so why not do away with it -altogether? That is exactly the plea I am making, and I think that is one reason why this particular tax should be done away with.
I would like to ask the parliamentary assistant two questions. What is the total revenue accruing to the funds of Canada through the imposition of duties on books? I would have liked to include in that a question as to the amount that would be lost through abolition of the sales tax, but at the moment I suppose I can only ask about the customs duties. My second question is, what are the four countries with which he said we had a special treaty in this regard?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My duties as parliamentary assistant here, I think, are to put through the items appearing in the schedules now before this house. I do not think it is part of my task to read, as I had to read, the existing tariff schedules to an hon. member who wants to make a long speech on books. I would have thought he would read the schedules before making that speech. The same is true in regard to revenue.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I have not asked the parliamentary assistant to read anything. I asked him a question. I asked him the revenue accruing to Canada through the importation of books, and I asked him the names of the four countries with which Canada has a special treaty in this regard. The parliamentary assistant seems to be particularly cantankerous tonight. On my last question he tried to cut me down. He is most unreasonable, as I see it. I want the information. What are we here for if we cannot get information?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: One of the simple reasons we are here is to get information from the many documents the government and the library provide hon. members. There is no item in this schedule dealing with books. The only item having to do with publications at all refers to publications of the United Nations and its agencies and publications of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and its agencies. There is no loss there because we have not been charging tariffs on these items. As far as the revenue on books is concerned, if the hon. member cannot dig it out of the publications supplied to him, all he has to do is put a question on the order paper, as he has done so often, and he will get the full story of the tariff on books and the countries with whom we have these agreements, together with the revenue last year or ten years ago or twenty years ago.

I think it is a pity we should have to be scolded. As a matter of fact I listened with great interest to what the parliamentary assistant had to say. I loved the sonorous way he rolled out the word "free", and I think we all received a little education. I think he should be glad of an opportunity to give us that education, and not scold us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Nothing was further from my mind than to scold the hon. member for Greenwood, because I will say he does a little research before he comes into the House of Commons on matters he intends to speak on.

I was as
ignorant as anyone else on this subject. Everything the parliamentary assistant said was interesting to me. I was glad to hear it, and I think we might all be glad that we received this bit of education, thanks to the hon. member for Saskatoon. I am glad personally.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If my job here is to give interesting information on all items which are not in the schedule now before this house, I could be here a long, long time. I do not think the hon. member for Greenwood would be so grateful for all the irrelevant information I might produce. I think my job here is to discuss the implications of these reductions in tariff which are proposed in this schedule.

I think the whole answer is that the parliamentary assistant has not explained the difficulty in which the hon. member for Saskatoon finds himself. It is the old story of the difference between theory and practice. If a university wishes to import these books true enough they come in duty free. If a professor imports them in his own name he pays the tariff, unless he has the foresight to go to his board and ask that they import them in their name on his behalf. There should not be that differentiation. If a book is free to the university it should be free to the professor in the university.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In my own fairly long
experience with universities most professors wanting books have the library acquire them, and in that case they are free.
If the professor pays for the book he should get it free of duty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In view of the communicative mood in which my hon. friend the parliamentary assistant finds himself I will give him a chance to give other information. I shall relate what I have to say to items such as 206a and 220b. There may other items in the group now before us which are also related to the question I have in mind. The question I wish to put to the parliamentary assistant is this. To what extent are there any tariff changes in the group of items now before us affecting drugs and medicines? I said this afternoon when we were on another item that at pages 1396 to 1398 of Hansard for April 9, 1952, would be found answers to questions of mine having to do with sales tax and tariff rates on drugs and medicines. Naturally I am not going to read to the parliamentary assistant now the long list of items on those three pages, but I would call
Customs Tariff
his attention to one item in particular. I take it from page 1397 of Hansard, under item 220, which is perhaps one of the most important items in relation to the question of duties on drugs and medicines.
Item 220 reads:
All medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations, compounded of more than one substance, including patent and proprietary preparations, tinctures, pills, powders, troches, lozenges, filled capsules, tablets, syrups, cordials, bitters, anodynes, tonics, plasters, liniments, salves, ointments, pastes, drops, waters, essences and oils, n.o.p.;
When dry, the British preferential tariff is 17J per cent; the most-favoured-nation tariff 20 per cent and the general tariff 25 per cent.
There is more to that item 220, but that is all I need to read at this time. I notice that item 220d is referred to in the schedule now before us, but there is no reference to item 220 itself. I should like to know whether consideration has been given to reducing this omnibus tariff on medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations. I do not know whether the parliamentary assistant has taken the trouble to look up the three pages of Hansard to which I referred. He will see that there is a long list there of items which the Minister of National Revenue, in his answer to my question, regarded as referring to drugs and medicines. I have tried to compare that list of items with the items in this group, although I confess that I have not taken every one and checked it. I hope the parliamentary assistant will not accuse me of not doing enough research on the matter, but I did not find many cases, if any, where the tariff has been reduced on so-called drugs and medicines.

speechtext: The one covering item in this schedule is 206a(3). You can see the class, so far as the item-

A year or two ago we had a discussion on the same problem in connection with antibiotics, whether or not it was worth while to encourage, by some tariff protection, the construction of plants to make

penicillin, aureomycin and these other antibiotics. In looking over item 220 I would say that almost all of those articles are of a class or kind made in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it possible to ascertain tonight, or shall I put it on the order paper, what the revenue is from an item like 220?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I certainly cannot tell the hon. member that tonight because item 220 is not here. There is a new item 220d for coating fluorescent lamps.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I notice that the official in
front of the parliamentary assistant is looking at a book. Can he find it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He is an official on tariffs, not of the Department of National Revenue which is the one that records statistics so far as revenue is concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I just want to say, as was pointed out this afternoon, that the cost of drugs and medicines to the Canadian people does seem to be increased far more than I think it should be by the imposition of the sales tax we were talking about this afternoon, and now by far too many duties on this long list of medicinal items. I certainly hope that the government will give further consideration to both of these pleas that we have made today, for the elimination of the sales tax on medicines and for reducing or eliminating tariff thereon.
Has the parliamentary assistant been able to get any information as to the revenue obtained by the federal government on drugs and medicines, in any form that the parliamentary assistant can give it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have here a report on trade in Canada for 1950 in which the classification is not by tariff items, but on these medicinal, chemical and pharmaceutical preparations- this does not include Canadian production which is the greater part of this field-total imports were almost $6 million, $5,892,000, and the tax paid was $1,154,000, which is a little less than 20 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the cost of the products produced in Canada would equal the cost of those brought in from the United States, plus the tariff.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Is that a statement or a
question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is a statement with which I am sure the parliamentary assistant agrees.

I should like to ask the minister a question on item 199h, on page 16,

concerning pots, boxes, bands, collars or protectors for plants. I have had very strong representations made to me by several of the greenhouse men and market gardeners in my constituency concerning this item. They request the elimination of the tariff, as it is not an item that is made in Canada at all and it is an essential item for the production of plants, flowers and other crops.
Now, I gather that the general tariff rate is 10 per cent, and there has been a substantial reduction which I am sure my constituents will be glad to see. I gather that the greater part of the importations-all of It is imported-comes under the item of the general tariff-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, all of it comes in under either most-favoured-nation or British preferential tariff rates.
I am glad to hear that. Then, it is virtually a removal of the tariff on this item.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant a question referring especially to item 848(1) and (2) on page 33. I judge that 848(2) is a new item covering materials for use in the manufacture of the goods enumerated in tariff item 848(1). Is that correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is new, yes, because out in your province there is the beginning of an industry in the manufacture of this oil well drilling equipment. We are now, therefore, extending the exemption which is given to most industries in Canada, that the primary products they use in manufacture shall be exempt or have low rates of duty.

I am glad to have that included. It will have a very material effect on stimulating the production of oilfield equipment in Canada. One point in item 848(1) is not clear. We have there a list of machinery and apparatus, which is free, including casing and tubing and drill pipe for use in connection with natural gas or oil wells. Does this free list cover steel or iron pipe used for gathering oil or gas for transportation or distribution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, it does not. That part is an old item. Actually, the change in the schedule is 848(2), materials for the use in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff item 848(1). The manufacturing process gets this special provision but not the transportation end, the movement away from the well in the pipe lines.
Can the parliamentary assistant advise me what the tariff is at present on iron or steel pipe for transmission?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Item 397, pipes and tubes, of wrought iron or steel, plain or coated, welded or seamless, with plain or processed ends: 15 per cent, the British preferential tariff; 22J per cent, the most-favoured-nation tariff; and 30 per cent, the general tariff.

In view of the fact that pipe used for transmission and the gathering of oil and gas is a material item in the cost of construction of pipe lines and in view of the fact that transmission is a material item in the cost of the oil or gas to the consumer, will the tariff board or the government consider placing line pipe or pipe for the transmission of oil or gas in the same category as pipe actually used in the boring of a well?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Consideration was given to that question three or four years ago and I believe there was actually an item placed in the tariff schedule resolution but it was withdrawn in the following bill because of the opposition of quite a number of western members to any increase in the tariff on pipe. However, consideration is given to all of these representations. There is, of course, quite a substantial pipe industry in Canada itself, using Canadian steel out of Hamilton, Algoma and Sydney.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall resolution 2 carry?

Just one more question, Mr. Chairman. The parliamentary assistant mentioned the fact that we have mills in Canada rolling iron pipe. I believe the maximum diameter of pipe that can be rolled in Canada is 16 inch, which is smaller than the diameter of pipe used for any large oil or gas pipe line such as those that are now contemplated east and west in Alberta. Inasmuch as pipe larger in diameter than 16 inches cannot be rolled in Canada, should not that larger pipe come into Canada from United States mills free of duty?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The government's policy at the moment is that it should not. Consideration can be given. The tariff on pipe at the moment is a measure of protection to those mills in eastern Canada. No doubt as the oil and gas industry develops, and there is going to be this greater demand for such pipe, the Canadian mills will, as they have in the past, extend to meet that demand. But at the moment there has been no change made in the tariff on such sized pipe.

speechtext: Shall this resolution carry?

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act to correct certain anomalies, to clarify the application of certain provisions and to make certain technical amendments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I should say just a word. This resolution does not give much in the way of detail because there is no general change in the rates or in the incidence of the taxes. As hon. members know, an overhaul of the succession duty law is needed. We had hoped to be able to bring forward a full revision for the consideration of hon. members at this time but it has not been possible to do this. There are, however, a few amendments of a technical nature which require immediate attention. These amendments are not matters of policy but are merely clarifying certain provisions of the law and removing certain anomalies. It is difficult to discuss them without the bill. They are almost entirely legal points such as those which the hon. member for Hamilton West raised in her speech in the budget debate. The minister will be putting through this bill. The resolution is just in effect a warning to members to the effect that there are going to be technical amendments made to the succession duty act, because of the experience in recent years, without changing the basic rates of duty or the levels.

Mr. Chairman, I was not prepared to speak upon this subject at the moment because I thought we were taking the income tax resolution first. However, in the amendments to the Dominion Succession Duty Act I hope that cognizance will be taken of the incidence of double taxation of which I spoke and of which I gave an example in my remarks on the budget. I believe this is a situation which is well known in the taxation

Dominion Succession Duty Act field and one which has long required some revision. If this is one of the points which it is intended to rectify, with the introduction of this resolution, I would be heartily in favour of it. In going into the matter I trust that not only this particular problem will be rectified but also the many others which are familiar to all of us in the field of succession duty and income tax incidence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Perhaps I should explain to the hon. member that she was quite right in saying that the list given last night indicated that the income tax resolution would come first. But since this is only a warning if we do get it through tonight it means that perhaps the bills based on the three resolutions can be circulated tomorrow and then we can start afresh on the fourth resolution, namely the income tax resolution. When the succession duties bill is in your hands you will be better able to see whether the points you have in mind are covered. The minister also told me to say that the usual period will intervene between the introduction of the income tax bill and the succession duty bill and discussion in the house. These are very technical bills requiring detailed study, unlike the excise tax and the customs tariff bills which are quite straightforward. There will be an interval of probably a week between the circulation tomorrow of the income tax and succession duty bills and the discussion in the house by the minister on second reading.

I hope that the anomaly with regard to the succession duties between the common law provinces and the province of Quebec will be considered when this bill is being brought down. I refer to the situation which at present exists whereby in the common law provinces, when a taxpayer dies, his estate for succession duty purposes is considered in toto and duties are levied on the entire estate whereas under the civil laws of the province of Quebec, when a taxpayer dies it is considered that half of his estate belongs to his wife and succession duties are levied on merely the half of the estate considered as belonging to him.
It appears to me that that is an anomaly which should be eradicated. I think that the situation under the Quebec law is a good one because it certainly provides for the widow a degree of security which is not found under the laws of the common law provinces. I feel that that is one of the points which might form the basis of discussion in a dominion-provincial conference so that succession duties shall be levied on an equal

basis throughout the entire dominion. I understand that unless there is a marriage contract in the province of Quebec the taxation as I have explained it is in force; but if there is a marriage contract, then of course the terms of that contract are valid. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that since we are discussing this very serious matter of succession duties, the double succession duties that are levied, particularly in the province of Ontario, consideration should be given so that succession duties shall be considered on the same basis throughout the entire dominion.

Has the
parliamentary assistant available the basic figures showing what the succession duty has yielded in the way of revenue during the course of the years it has been running? Perhaps I could wait until we have the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The amount is shown in the budget papers. My recollection is that it was $32 million last year-that is federal succession duty, of course. Pardon me, the forecast of revenue in the coming year is $43 million. The rates of course are not changed. Last year it was $38 million; this year $43 million; and the forecast for next year is also $43 million.

The parliamentary assistant said that this resolution was a warning. I think it should be a warning against having resolutions such as this. It reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act-
If it stopped there it would have been much clearer and much better. It then goes on to say:
-to correct certain anomalies.-
Which I presume is the amendment. Then it continues:
-to clarify the application of certain provisions and to make certain technical amendments.
I think it is a warning against having any resolution such as this, Mr. Chairman. We would be much better off if we did not have any resolution such as this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That very point was discussed as to whether a resolution was needed at all. I used the word "warning" perhaps in a colloquial sense; but it was an indication to the house that a tax measure or a money measure was coming. Since this involves changes in the law without a change in the rate or in the incidence of the tax doubt was expressed as to whether a resolution was needed at all. If we had no resolution we might have been subjected to the criticism

that we were bringing in a change in a tax bill without a resolution. If we had left it as an amendment to the Dominion Succession Duty Act, then there would be a question in hon. members' minds that perhaps we were going to change the rate. They would have said: if they are not going to change the rate, why do they not say so; this was the decision made, and the resolution is an indication to the house that the succession duty act is to be amended, but not amended in a way to levy new tax changes, changing the rates or changing the incidence.

It would have been better simply to have said: "Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act but not to change the rates." As it is, it is the height of vague ambiguity.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue in ways and means with the last budget resolution concerning income tax. If we have time we shall take up the resolution in the name of the Minister of National Defence. It was discussed yesterday and the debate was adjourned by the hon. member for Nanaimo; then the resolution in the name of the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning a treaty of peace between Canada and Japan; next, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys concerning the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; then if we have more time we shall take up a little bill of the Minister of Justice to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act, and then Bill No. 93 to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.
